<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Foro_Romano_visto_dai_Musei_Capitolini_Roma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Foro_Romano_visto_dai_Musei_Capitolini_Roma.jpg/250px-Foro_Romano_visto_dai_Musei_Capitolini_Roma.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="130" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Foro_Romano_visto_dai_Musei_Capitolini_Roma.jpg/500px-Foro_Romano_visto_dai_Musei_Capitolini_Roma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="13800" data-file-height="7160"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Roman_Forum" title="Roman Forum">Roman Forum</a> contains the ruins of the buildings that represented the political, legal, religious and economic centre of ancient Rome, constituting the "nerve centre" of all Roman civilisation.<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>After the foundation by Romulus (according to a legend),<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196473_33-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196473-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome was ruled for a period of 244 years by a <a href="/wiki/Monarchy" title="Monarchy">monarchy</a>. The first rulers were of <a href="/wiki/Latins_(Italic_tribe)" title="Latins (Italic tribe)">Latin</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sabines" title="Sabines">Sabine</a> origin, and later ones were <a href="/wiki/Etruscans" class="mw-redirect" title="Etruscans">Etruscan</a>. The tradition handed down seven kings: <a href="/wiki/Romulus" title="Romulus">Romulus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Numa_Pompilius" title="Numa Pompilius">Numa Pompilius</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tullus_Hostilius" title="Tullus Hostilius">Tullus Hostilius</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ancus_Marcius" title="Ancus Marcius">Ancus Marcius</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tarquinius_Priscus" class="mw-redirect" title="Tarquinius Priscus">Tarquinius Priscus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Servius_Tullius" title="Servius Tullius">Servius Tullius</a> and <a href="/wiki/Lucius_Tarquinius_Superbus" title="Lucius Tarquinius Superbus">Lucius Tarquinius Superbus</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196473_33-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196473-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 509 BC, the Romans expelled the last king from their city and established an <a href="/wiki/Oligarchy" title="Oligarchy">oligarchic</a> <a href="/wiki/Republic" title="Republic">republic</a> led by two annually elected <a href="/wiki/Roman_consul" title="Roman consul">consuls</a>. Rome then began a period characterised by internal struggles between <a href="/wiki/Patrician_(ancient_Rome)" title="Patrician (ancient Rome)">patricians</a> (aristocrats) and <a href="/wiki/Plebs" class="mw-redirect" title="Plebs">plebeians</a> (small landowners), and by constant warfare against the populations of central Italy: Etruscans, Latins, <a href="/wiki/Volsci" title="Volsci">Volsci</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aequi" title="Aequi">Aequi</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Marsi" title="Marsi">Marsi</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196477_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196477-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After becoming master of <a href="/wiki/Latium" title="Latium">Latium</a>, Rome led several wars (against the <a href="/wiki/Gauls" title="Gauls">Gauls</a>, <a href="/wiki/Osci" title="Osci">Osci</a>-<a href="/wiki/Samnites" title="Samnites">Samnites</a> and the Greek colony of <a href="/wiki/Taranto" title="Taranto">Taranto</a>, allied with <a href="/wiki/Pyrrhus_of_Epirus" title="Pyrrhus of Epirus">Pyrrhus</a>, king of <a href="/wiki/Epirus" title="Epirus">Epirus</a>) whose result was the conquest of the <a href="/wiki/Italian_peninsula" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian peninsula">Italian peninsula</a>, from the central area up to <a href="/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia">Magna Graecia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196479_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196479-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The 3rd and 4th century BC saw the establishment of Roman hegemony over the <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean" class="mw-redirect" title="Mediterranean">Mediterranean</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</a> through the three <a href="/wiki/Punic_Wars" title="Punic Wars">Punic Wars</a> (264–146 BC) fought against <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Carthage" title="Ancient Carthage">Carthage</a> and the three <a href="/wiki/Macedonian_Wars" title="Macedonian Wars">Macedonian Wars</a> (212–168 BC) against <a href="/wiki/Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom)" title="Macedonia (ancient kingdom)">Macedonia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196481–83_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196481–83-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The first <a href="/wiki/Roman_province" title="Roman province">Roman provinces</a> were established at this time: <a href="/wiki/Sicilia_(Roman_province)" title="Sicilia (Roman province)">Sicily</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sardinia_and_Corsica" title="Sardinia and Corsica">Sardinia and Corsica</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hispania" title="Hispania">Hispania</a>, <a href="/wiki/Macedonia_(Roman_province)" title="Macedonia (Roman province)">Macedonia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Achaea_(Roman_province)" class="mw-redirect" title="Achaea (Roman province)">Achaea</a> and <a href="/wiki/Africa_(Roman_province)" title="Africa (Roman province)">Africa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196481–85_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196481–85-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>From the beginning of the 2nd century BC, power was contested between two groups of aristocrats: the <a href="/wiki/Optimates" class="mw-redirect" title="Optimates">optimates</a>, representing the conservative part of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_senate" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman senate">Senate</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Populares" class="mw-redirect" title="Populares">populares</a>, who relied on the help of the <a href="/wiki/Plebs" class="mw-redirect" title="Plebs">plebs</a> (urban lower class) to gain power. In the same period, the bankruptcy of the small farmers and the establishment of large slave estates caused large-scale migration to the city. The continuous warfare led to the establishment of a professional army, which turned out to be more loyal to its generals than to the republic. Because of this, in the late 2nd and early 1st century BC there were several conflicts both abroad and internally: after the failed attempt of social reform of the populares <a href="/wiki/Tiberius_Gracchus" title="Tiberius Gracchus">Tiberius</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gaius_Gracchus" title="Gaius Gracchus">Gaius Gracchus</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and the war against <a href="/wiki/Jugurtha" title="Jugurtha">Jugurtha</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489_43-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> there was <a href="/wiki/Sulla%27s_civil_war" title="Sulla's civil war">a civil war</a> from which the general <a href="/wiki/Sulla" title="Sulla">Sulla</a> emerged victorious.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489_43-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196489-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/Third_Servile_War" title="Third Servile War">major slave revolt</a> under <a href="/wiki/Spartacus" title="Spartacus">Spartacus</a> followed,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and then the establishment of the <a href="/wiki/First_Triumvirate" title="First Triumvirate">first Triumvirate</a> with <a href="/wiki/Julius_Caesar" title="Julius Caesar">Caesar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pompey" title="Pompey">Pompey</a> and <a href="/wiki/Marcus_Licinius_Crassus" title="Marcus Licinius Crassus">Crassus</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491_44-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Caesar's conquest of <a href="/wiki/Gaul" title="Gaul">Gaul</a> made him immensely powerful and popular, which led to a <a href="/wiki/Caesar%27s_Civil_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Caesar's Civil War">civil war</a> against the Senate and Pompey. After his victory, Caesar established himself as <a href="/wiki/Dictator_perpetuo" title="Dictator perpetuo">dictator for life</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491_44-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196491-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> His assassination in 44 BC led to a <a href="/wiki/Second_Triumvirate" title="Second Triumvirate">second Triumvirate</a> among <a href="/wiki/Octavian" class="mw-redirect" title="Octavian">Octavian</a> (Caesar's grandnephew and heir), <a href="/wiki/Mark_Antony" title="Mark Antony">Mark Antony</a> and <a href="/wiki/Lepidus" title="Lepidus">Lepidus</a>, and to a <a href="/wiki/War_of_Actium" title="War of Actium">final civil war</a> between Octavian and Antony.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196493_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196493-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Empire">Empire</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Palatine_Hill_from_across_the_Circus_Maximus_April_2019.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Palatine_Hill_from_across_the_Circus_Maximus_April_2019.jpg/250px-Palatine_Hill_from_across_the_Circus_Maximus_April_2019.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Palatine_Hill_from_across_the_Circus_Maximus_April_2019.jpg/500px-Palatine_Hill_from_across_the_Circus_Maximus_April_2019.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648"></a><figcaption>The Ancient-Imperial-Roman palaces of the Palatine, a series of palaces located in the <a href="/wiki/Palatine_Hill" title="Palatine Hill">Palatine Hill</a>, express power and wealth of emperors from Augustus until the 4th century.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Trajan%27s_Market,_Rome,_Italy.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Trajan%27s_Market%2C_Rome%2C_Italy.jpg/250px-Trajan%27s_Market%2C_Rome%2C_Italy.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Trajan%27s_Market%2C_Rome%2C_Italy.jpg/500px-Trajan%27s_Market%2C_Rome%2C_Italy.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4612" data-file-height="3062"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Imperial_fora" title="Imperial fora">Imperial fora</a> belong to a series of <i>monumental fora</i> (public squares) constructed in Rome by the emperors. Also seen in the image is <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Market" title="Trajan's Market">Trajan's Market</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:D%C3%A9tail_de_la_maquette_de_Rome_%C3%A0_l%C3%A9poque_de_Constantin_(5840455090).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/D%C3%A9tail_de_la_maquette_de_Rome_%C3%A0_l%C3%A9poque_de_Constantin_%285840455090%29.jpg/250px-D%C3%A9tail_de_la_maquette_de_Rome_%C3%A0_l%C3%A9poque_de_Constantin_%285840455090%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/D%C3%A9tail_de_la_maquette_de_Rome_%C3%A0_l%C3%A9poque_de_Constantin_%285840455090%29.jpg/500px-D%C3%A9tail_de_la_maquette_de_Rome_%C3%A0_l%C3%A9poque_de_Constantin_%285840455090%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200"></a><figcaption>Model of Imperial Rome at the <a href="/wiki/Museum_of_Roman_Civilization" title="Museum of Roman Civilization">Museum of Roman Civilization</a> in Rome. The <a href="/wiki/Temple_of_Claudius" title="Temple of Claudius">Temple of Claudius</a> is situated to the south (left) of the <a href="/wiki/Colosseum" title="Colosseum">Colosseum</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 27 BC, Octavian was named <i><a href="/wiki/Augustus_(title)" title="Augustus (title)">Augustus</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Princeps" title="Princeps">princeps</a></i>, founding the <a href="/wiki/Principate" title="Principate">principate</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Diarchy" title="Diarchy">diarchy</a> between the <i>princeps</i> and the senate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196493_45-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196493-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Over time, the new monarch came to be known as the <i><a href="/wiki/Imperator" title="Imperator">imperator</a></i> (hence <a href="/wiki/Roman_emperor" title="Roman emperor">emperor</a>), meaning "commander".<sup id="cite_ref-SimonHornblower_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SimonHornblower-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the reign of <a href="/wiki/Nero" title="Nero">Nero</a>, two thirds of the city was ruined after the <a href="/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome" title="Great Fire of Rome">Great Fire of Rome</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians_in_the_Roman_Empire" title="Persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire">persecution of Christians</a> commenced.<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome's empire reached its greatest expansion in the second century under the Emperor <a href="/wiki/Trajan" title="Trajan">Trajan</a>. Rome was known as the <a href="/wiki/Caput_Mundi" title="Caput Mundi">caput Mundi</a>, i.e. the capital of the known world, an expression which had already been used in the Republican period. During its first two centuries, the empire was ruled by emperors of the <a href="/wiki/Julio-Claudian_dynasty" title="Julio-Claudian dynasty">Julio-Claudian</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196497_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196497-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Flavian_dynasty" title="Flavian dynasty">Flavian</a> (who built an eponymous amphitheatre known as the <a href="/wiki/Colosseum" title="Colosseum">Colosseum</a>),<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196497_50-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196497-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Antonine_dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Antonine dynasty">Antonine</a> dynasties.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196499_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196499-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This time was also characterised by the spread of the Christian religion, preached by <a href="/wiki/Jesus_Christ" class="mw-redirect" title="Jesus Christ">Jesus Christ</a> in <a href="/wiki/Judea" title="Judea">Judea</a> in the first half of the first century (under <a href="/wiki/Tiberius" title="Tiberius">Tiberius</a>) and popularised by his <a href="/wiki/Apostles_in_the_New_Testament" title="Apostles in the New Testament">apostles</a> through the empire and beyond.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964107_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964107-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Antonine age is considered the zenith of the Empire, whose territory ranged from the <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean" title="Atlantic Ocean">Atlantic Ocean</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Euphrates" title="Euphrates">Euphrates</a> and from <a href="/wiki/Great_Britain" title="Great Britain">Britain</a> to <a href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196499_51-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann196499-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum_in_Rome-April_2007-1-_copie_2B.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Colosseum_in_Rome-April_2007-1-_copie_2B.jpg/250px-Colosseum_in_Rome-April_2007-1-_copie_2B.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Colosseum_in_Rome-April_2007-1-_copie_2B.jpg/500px-Colosseum_in_Rome-April_2007-1-_copie_2B.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4827" data-file-height="2833"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Colosseum" title="Colosseum">Colosseum</a> at dusk</figcaption></figure>
<p>After the end of the <a href="/wiki/Severan_dynasty" title="Severan dynasty">Severan dynasty</a> in AD 235, the Empire entered into a 50-year period known as the <a href="/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century" title="Crisis of the Third Century">Crisis of the Third Century</a>, during which numerous generals fought for power and the central authority in Rome weakened dramatically. Around the same time, the <a href="/wiki/Plague_of_Cyprian" title="Plague of Cyprian">Plague of Cyprian</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 250–270) afflicted the Mediterranean.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Instability caused economic deterioration, and there was a rapid rise in inflation as the government debased the currency in order to meet expenses. The <a href="/wiki/Germanic_tribes" class="mw-redirect" title="Germanic tribes">Germanic tribes</a> along the Rhine and north of the Balkans made serious uncoordinated incursions that were more like giant raiding parties rather than attempts to settle. The <a href="/wiki/Sasanian_Empire" title="Sasanian Empire">Persian Empire</a> invaded from the east several times during the 230s to 260s but were eventually defeated.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The civil wars ended in 285 with the final victory of <a href="/wiki/Diocletian" title="Diocletian">Diocletian</a>, who undertook the restoration of the State. He ended the <a href="/wiki/Principate" title="Principate">Principate</a> and introduced a new authoritarian model known as the <a href="/wiki/Dominate" title="Dominate">Dominate</a>, derived from his title of <i>dominus</i> ("lord"). His most marked feature was the unprecedented intervention of the State down to the city level: whereas the State had submitted a tax demand to a city and allowed it to allocate the charges, from his reign the State did this down to the village level. In a vain attempt to control inflation, he imposed <a href="/wiki/Price_controls" title="Price controls">price controls</a> which did not last.
</p><p>Diocletian divided the empire in 286, ruling over the eastern half from <a href="/wiki/Nicomedia" title="Nicomedia">Nicomedia</a>, while his co-emperor <a href="/wiki/Maximian" title="Maximian">Maximian</a> ruled the western half from <a href="/wiki/Mediolanum" title="Mediolanum">Mediolanum</a> (when not on the move).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101_54-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The empire was further divided in 293, when Diocletian named two <a href="/wiki/Caesar_(title)" title="Caesar (title)">caesar</a>, one for each <a href="/wiki/Augustus_(title)" title="Augustus (title)">augustus</a> (emperor). Diocletian tried to turn into a system of non-dynastic succession, similar to the Antonine dynasty. Upon abdication in 305, both caesars succeeded and they, in turn, appointed two colleagues for themselves.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101_54-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964101-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, a <a href="/wiki/Civil_wars_of_the_Tetrarchy" title="Civil wars of the Tetrarchy">series of civil wars</a> between rival claimants to power resulted in the unification of the empire under <a href="/wiki/Constantine_the_Great" title="Constantine the Great">Constantine the Great</a> in 324. Hereditary succession was restored, but the east–west division was maintained. Constantine undertook a major reform of the bureaucracy, not by changing the structure but by rationalising the competencies of the several ministries. The so-called <a href="/wiki/Edict_of_Milan" title="Edict of Milan">Edict of Milan</a> of 313, actually a fragment of a letter from his co-emperor <a href="/wiki/Licinius" title="Licinius">Licinius</a> to the governors of the eastern provinces, granted freedom of worship to everyone, including Christians, and ordered the restoration of confiscated church properties upon petition to the newly created vicars of dioceses. He funded the building of several churches and allowed clergy to act as arbitrators in civil suits (a measure that did not outlast him but which was restored in part much later). In 330, he transformed <a href="/wiki/Byzantium" title="Byzantium">Byzantium</a> into <a href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</a>, which became his new capital. However, it was not officially anything more than an imperial residence like <a href="/wiki/Milan" title="Milan">Milan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Trier" title="Trier">Trier</a> or <a href="/wiki/Nicomedia" title="Nicomedia">Nicomedia</a> until given a city prefect in 359 by <a href="/wiki/Constantius_II" title="Constantius II">Constantius II</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964103_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964103-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Constantine, following Diocletian's reforms, regionalised the administration, which fundamentally changed the way it was governed by creating regional dioceses. The existence of regional fiscal units from 286 served as the model for this unprecedented innovation.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The emperor quickened the process of removing military command from governors. Henceforth, civilian administration and military command would be separate. He gave governors more fiscal duties and placed them in charge of the army logistical support system as an attempt to control it by removing the support system from its control.
</p><p>Christianity in the form of the Nicene Creed became the official religion of the empire in 380, via the <a href="/wiki/Edict_of_Thessalonica" title="Edict of Thessalonica">Edict of Thessalonica</a> issued in the name of three emperors – Gratian, Valentinian II, and <a href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</a> – with Theodosius clearly the driving force behind it. He was the last emperor of a unified empire: after his death in 395, his young children, <a href="/wiki/Honorius_(emperor)" class="mw-redirect" title="Honorius (emperor)">Honorius</a> and <a href="/wiki/Arcadius" title="Arcadius">Arcadius</a>, inherited the <a href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">western</a> and <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Eastern Roman Empire">eastern</a> empires respectively. The seat of government in the Western Roman Empire was transferred to <a href="/wiki/Ravenna" title="Ravenna">Ravenna</a> in 408, but from 450 the emperors mostly resided in Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Sack_of_Rome_by_the_Visigoths_on_24_August_410_by_JN_Sylvestre_1890.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Sack_of_Rome_by_the_Visigoths_on_24_August_410_by_JN_Sylvestre_1890.jpg/250px-Sack_of_Rome_by_the_Visigoths_on_24_August_410_by_JN_Sylvestre_1890.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="445" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Sack_of_Rome_by_the_Visigoths_on_24_August_410_by_JN_Sylvestre_1890.jpg/500px-Sack_of_Rome_by_the_Visigoths_on_24_August_410_by_JN_Sylvestre_1890.jpg 2x" data-file-width="841" data-file-height="1498"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Visigoths" title="Visigoths">Visigoths</a> <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)" title="Sack of Rome (410)">sacking Rome in 410</a>, by <a href="/wiki/Joseph-No%C3%ABl_Sylvestre" title="Joseph-Noël Sylvestre">Joseph-Noël Sylvestre</a> (1890), the first time in <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome, which had lost its central role in the administration of the empire, <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)" title="Sack of Rome (410)">was sacked in 410</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Visigoths" title="Visigoths">Visigoths</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Alaric_I" title="Alaric I">Alaric I</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964115_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964115-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> but very little physical damage was done, most of which was repaired. What could not be so easily replaced were portable items such as artwork in precious metals and items for domestic use (loot). The popes embellished the city with large basilicas, such as <a href="/wiki/Santa_Maria_Maggiore" title="Santa Maria Maggiore">Santa Maria Maggiore</a> (with the collaboration of the emperors). The population of the city had fallen from 800,000 to 450–500,000 by the time the city was sacked in 455 by <a href="/wiki/Genseric" class="mw-redirect" title="Genseric">Genseric</a>, king of the <a href="/wiki/Vandals" title="Vandals">Vandals</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964117_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The weak emperors of the fifth century could not stop the decay, leading to the deposition of <a href="/wiki/Romulus_Augustus" class="mw-redirect" title="Romulus Augustus">Romulus Augustus</a>, who resided on Ravenna, on 4 September 476. This marked the end of the <a href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">Western Roman Empire</a> and, for many historians, the beginning of the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964103_55-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinderHilgemann1964103-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The decline of the city's population was caused by the loss of grain shipments from North Africa, from 440 onward, and the unwillingness of the senatorial class to maintain donations to support a population that was too large for the resources available. Even so, strenuous efforts were made to maintain the monumental centre, the palatine, and the largest baths, which continued to function until the Gothic siege of 537. The large baths of Constantine on the Quirinale were even repaired in 443, and the extent of the damage exaggerated and dramatised.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>However, the city gave an appearance overall of shabbiness and decay because of the large abandoned areas due to population decline. The population declined to 500,000 by 452 and 100,000 by AD 500 (perhaps larger, though no certain figure can be known). After the Gothic siege of 537, the population dropped to 30,000 but had risen to 90,000 by the papacy of <a href="/wiki/Pope_Gregory_I" title="Pope Gregory I">Gregory the Great</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The population decline coincided with the general collapse of urban life in the West in the fifth and sixth centuries, with few exceptions. Subsidized state grain distributions to the poorer members of society continued right through the sixth century and probably prevented the population from falling further.<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The figure of 450,000–500,000 is based on the amount of pork, 3,629,000 lbs. distributed to poorer Romans during five winter months at the rate of five Roman lbs per person per month, enough for 145,000 persons or 1/4 or 1/3 of the total population.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Grain distribution to 80,000 ticket holders at the same time suggests 400,000 (Augustus set the number at 200,000 or one-fifth of the population).
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Middle_Ages">Middle Ages</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire" title="Fall of the Western Roman Empire">Fall of the Western Roman Empire</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Genseric_sacking_rome_456.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Genseric_sacking_rome_456.jpg/250px-Genseric_sacking_rome_456.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="186" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Genseric_sacking_rome_456.jpg/500px-Genseric_sacking_rome_456.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2660" data-file-height="1977"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Vandals" title="Vandals">Vandals</a> <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455)" title="Sack of Rome (455)">sacking Rome in 455</a>, by <a href="/wiki/Karl_Briullov" class="mw-redirect" title="Karl Briullov">Karl Briullov</a> (1830s)</figcaption></figure>
<p>After the <a href="/wiki/Decline_of_the_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Decline of the Roman Empire">fall of the Western Roman Empire</a> in AD 476, Rome was first under the control of <a href="/wiki/Odoacer" title="Odoacer">Odoacer</a> and then became part of the <a href="/wiki/Ostrogothic_Kingdom" title="Ostrogothic Kingdom">Ostrogothic Kingdom</a> before returning to <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">East Roman</a> control after the <a href="/wiki/Gothic_War_(535%E2%80%93554)" title="Gothic War (535–554)">Gothic War</a>, which devastated the city <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(546)" title="Sack of Rome (546)">in 546</a> and <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Rome_(549%E2%80%93550)" title="Siege of Rome (549–550)">550</a>. Its population declined from more than a million in AD 210 to 500,000 in AD 273<sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> to 35,000 after the Gothic War (535–554),<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> reducing the sprawling city to groups of inhabited buildings interspersed among large areas of ruins, vegetation, vineyards and market gardens.<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is generally thought the population of the city until AD 300 was 1 million (estimates range from 2 million to 750,000) declining to 750–800,000 in AD 400, then 450–500,000 in AD 450 and down to 80–100,000 in AD 500 (though it may have been twice this).<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The Bishop of Rome, called the <a href="/wiki/Pope" title="Pope">Pope</a>, was important since the early days of Christianity because of the martyrdom of both the apostles <a href="/wiki/Simon_Peter" class="mw-redirect" title="Simon Peter">Peter</a> and <a href="/wiki/Paul_of_Tarsus" class="mw-redirect" title="Paul of Tarsus">Paul</a> there. The Bishops of Rome were also seen (and still are seen by Catholics) as the successors of Peter, who is considered the first Bishop of Rome. The city thus became of increasing importance as the centre of the <a href="/wiki/Catholic_Church" title="Catholic Church">Catholic Church</a>.
</p><p>After the <a href="/wiki/Lombard_invasion_of_Italy#Invasion_and_conquest_of_the_Italian_peninsula" class="mw-redirect" title="Lombard invasion of Italy">Lombard invasion of Italy</a> (569–572), the city remained nominally Byzantine, but in reality, the popes pursued a policy of equilibrium between the <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantines</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Franks" title="Franks">Franks</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Lombards" title="Lombards">Lombards</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 729, the Lombard king <a href="/wiki/Liutprand,_King_of_the_Lombards" title="Liutprand, King of the Lombards">Liutprand</a> donated the north Latium town of <a href="/wiki/Sutri" title="Sutri">Sutri</a> to the Church, starting its <a href="/wiki/Temporalities" title="Temporalities">temporal</a> power.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 756, <a href="/wiki/Pepin_the_Short" title="Pepin the Short">Pepin the Short</a>, after having defeated the Lombards, gave the Pope temporal jurisdiction over the <a href="/wiki/Duchy_of_Rome" title="Duchy of Rome">Duchy of Rome</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Exarchate_of_Ravenna" title="Exarchate of Ravenna">Exarchate of Ravenna</a>, thus creating the <a href="/wiki/Papal_States" title="Papal States">Papal States</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since this period, three powers tried to rule the city: the pope, the nobility (together with the chiefs of militias, the judges, the Senate and the populace), and the Frankish king, as king of the Lombards, patricius, and Emperor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These three parties (theocratic, republican, and imperial) were a characteristic of Roman life during the entire Middle Ages.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On Christmas night of 800, <a href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</a> was crowned in Rome as <a href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor" title="Holy Roman Emperor">Emperor</a> by <a href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_III" title="Pope Leo III">Pope Leo III</a>: on that occasion, the city hosted for the first time the two powers whose struggle for control was to be a constant of the Middle Ages.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519_68-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192519-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This event marks the beginning of the <a href="/wiki/Carolingian_Empire" title="Carolingian Empire">Carolingian Empire</a>, the first phase of the <a href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</a>.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Detail_coronation_Charles_the_Great_(Francis_1st_of_France)_by_Pope_Leo_III_(Leo_X)_Vatican_11.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Detail_coronation_Charles_the_Great_%28Francis_1st_of_France%29_by_Pope_Leo_III_%28Leo_X%29_Vatican_11.jpg/250px-Detail_coronation_Charles_the_Great_%28Francis_1st_of_France%29_by_Pope_Leo_III_%28Leo_X%29_Vatican_11.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="222" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Detail_coronation_Charles_the_Great_%28Francis_1st_of_France%29_by_Pope_Leo_III_%28Leo_X%29_Vatican_11.jpg/500px-Detail_coronation_Charles_the_Great_%28Francis_1st_of_France%29_by_Pope_Leo_III_%28Leo_X%29_Vatican_11.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3072" data-file-height="2731"></a><figcaption>Detail from an illustration by <a href="/wiki/Raffaello_Sanzio_da_Urbino" class="mw-redirect" title="Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino">Raphael</a>, portraying the crowning of <a href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</a> in <a href="/wiki/Old_Saint_Peter%27s_Basilica" class="mw-redirect" title="Old Saint Peter's Basilica">Old Saint Peter's Basilica</a>, on 25 December 800</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 846, Muslim Arabs <a href="/wiki/Arab_raid_against_Rome" title="Arab raid against Rome">unsuccessfully stormed the city's walls</a>, but managed to loot <a href="/wiki/Old_St._Peter%27s_Basilica" title="Old St. Peter's Basilica">St. Peter</a>'s and St. Paul's basilica, both outside the city wall.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After the decay of <a href="/wiki/Carolingian_Empire" title="Carolingian Empire">Carolingian power</a>, Rome fell prey to feudal chaos: several noble families fought against the pope, the emperor, and each other. These were the times of <a href="/wiki/Theodora_(senatrix)" title="Theodora (senatrix)">Theodora</a> and her daughter <a href="/wiki/Marozia" title="Marozia">Marozia</a>, concubines and mothers of several popes, and of <a href="/wiki/Crescentius_the_Younger" title="Crescentius the Younger">Crescentius</a>, a powerful feudal lord, who fought against the Emperors <a href="/wiki/Otto_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Otto II">Otto II</a> and <a href="/wiki/Otto_III" class="mw-redirect" title="Otto III">Otto III</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The scandals of this period forced the papacy to reform itself: the election of the pope was reserved to the cardinals, and reform of the clergy was attempted. The driving force behind this renewal was the monk <a href="/wiki/Ildebrando_da_Soana" class="mw-redirect" title="Ildebrando da Soana">Ildebrando da Soana</a>, who once elected pope under the name of <a href="/wiki/Pope_Gregory_VII" title="Pope Gregory VII">Gregory VII</a> became involved into the <a href="/wiki/Investiture_Controversy" title="Investiture Controversy">Investiture Controversy</a> against Emperor <a href="/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor" title="Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor">Henry IV</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520_70-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Subsequently, Rome <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(1084)" title="Sack of Rome (1084)">was sacked and burned</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Normans" title="Normans">Normans</a> under <a href="/wiki/Robert_Guiscard" title="Robert Guiscard">Robert Guiscard</a> who had entered the city in support of the Pope, then besieged in <a href="/wiki/Castel_Sant%27Angelo" title="Castel Sant'Angelo">Castel Sant'Angelo</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520_70-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During this period, the city was autonomously ruled by a <i>senatore</i> or <i>patrizio</i>. In the 12th century, this administration, like other European cities, evolved into the <a href="/wiki/Medieval_commune" title="Medieval commune">commune</a>, a new form of social organisation controlled by the new wealthy classes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520_70-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192520-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Pope <a href="/wiki/Lucius_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Lucius II">Lucius II</a> fought against the Roman commune, and the struggle was continued by his successor <a href="/wiki/Pope_Eugenius_III" class="mw-redirect" title="Pope Eugenius III">Pope Eugenius III</a>: by this stage, the commune, allied with the aristocracy, was supported by <a href="/wiki/Arnaldo_da_Brescia" class="mw-redirect" title="Arnaldo da Brescia">Arnaldo da Brescia</a>, a monk who was a religious and social reformer.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After the pope's death, Arnaldo was taken prisoner by <a href="/wiki/Adrianus_IV" class="mw-redirect" title="Adrianus IV">Adrianus IV</a>, which marked the end of the commune's autonomy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Under <a href="/wiki/Pope_Innocent_III" title="Pope Innocent III">Pope Innocent III</a>, whose reign marked the apogee of the papacy, the commune liquidated the senate, and replaced it with a <i>Senatore</i>, who was subject to the pope.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In this period, the papacy played a role of secular importance in <a href="/wiki/Western_Europe" title="Western Europe">Western Europe</a>, often acting as arbitrators between Christian <a href="/wiki/Monarch" title="Monarch">monarchs</a> and exercising additional political powers.<sup id="cite_ref-Faus_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Faus-72"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Papal_Arbitration_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Papal_Arbitration-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 1266, <a href="/wiki/Charles_of_Anjou" class="mw-redirect" title="Charles of Anjou">Charles of Anjou</a>, who was heading south to fight the <a href="/wiki/Hohenstaufen" title="Hohenstaufen">Hohenstaufen</a> on behalf of the pope, was appointed Senator. Charles founded the <a href="/wiki/Sapienza_University_of_Rome" title="Sapienza University of Rome">Sapienza</a>, the university of Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that period the pope died, and the cardinals, summoned in <a href="/wiki/Viterbo" title="Viterbo">Viterbo</a>, could not agree on his successor. This angered the people of the city, who then unroofed the building where they met and imprisoned them until they had nominated the new pope; this marked the birth of the <a href="/wiki/Conclave" title="Conclave">conclave</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In this period the city was also shattered by continuous fights between the aristocratic families: <a href="/wiki/Annibaldi_family" title="Annibaldi family">Annibaldi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Caetani" title="Caetani">Caetani</a>, <a href="/wiki/Colonna_family" title="Colonna family">Colonna</a>, <a href="/wiki/Orsini_family" title="Orsini family">Orsini</a>, <a href="/wiki/Conti_di_Segni" title="Conti di Segni">Conti</a>, nested in their fortresses built above ancient Roman edifices, fought each other to control the papacy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Giorgio_Vasar_retour_id%C3%A9alis%C3%A9_de_Gr%C3%A9goire_XI_%C3%A0_Rome.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Giorgio_Vasar_retour_id%C3%A9alis%C3%A9_de_Gr%C3%A9goire_XI_%C3%A0_Rome.jpg/250px-Giorgio_Vasar_retour_id%C3%A9alis%C3%A9_de_Gr%C3%A9goire_XI_%C3%A0_Rome.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="189" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Giorgio_Vasar_retour_id%C3%A9alis%C3%A9_de_Gr%C3%A9goire_XI_%C3%A0_Rome.jpg/500px-Giorgio_Vasar_retour_id%C3%A9alis%C3%A9_de_Gr%C3%A9goire_XI_%C3%A0_Rome.jpg 2x" data-file-width="846" data-file-height="640"></a><figcaption>Pope <a href="/wiki/Gregory_XI" class="mw-redirect" title="Gregory XI">Gregory XI</a> returned to Rome in 1376 and ended the <a href="/wiki/Avignon_Papacy" title="Avignon Papacy">Avignon Papacy</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Pope_Boniface_VIII" title="Pope Boniface VIII">Pope Boniface VIII</a>, born Caetani, was the last pope to fight for the church's <a href="/w/index.php?title=Universal_domain&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Universal domain (page does not exist)">universal domain</a>; he proclaimed a crusade against the <a href="/wiki/Colonna_family" title="Colonna family">Colonna family</a> and, in 1300, called for the first <a href="/wiki/Jubilee_(Christianity)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jubilee (Christianity)">Jubilee of Christianity</a>, which brought millions of <a href="/wiki/Christian_pilgrimage" title="Christian pilgrimage">pilgrims</a> to Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, his hopes were crushed by the French king <a href="/wiki/Philip_IV_of_France" title="Philip IV of France">Philip the Fair</a>, who took him prisoner and held him hostage for three days at <a href="/wiki/Anagni" title="Anagni">Anagni</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521_71-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192521-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Pope was able to return to Rome, but died a month later, it was said of shock and grief. Afterwards, a new pope faithful to the French was elected, and the papacy was <a href="/wiki/Avignon_papacy" class="mw-redirect" title="Avignon papacy">briefly relocated</a> to <a href="/wiki/Avignon" title="Avignon">Avignon</a> (1309–1377).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During this period Rome was neglected, until a plebeian man, <a href="/wiki/Cola_di_Rienzo" title="Cola di Rienzo">Cola di Rienzo</a>, came to power.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An idealist and a lover of ancient Rome, Cola dreamed about a rebirth of the Roman Empire: after assuming power with the title of <i><a href="/wiki/Tribune" title="Tribune">Tribuno</a></i>, his reforms were rejected by the populace.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Forced to flee, Cola returned as part of the entourage of Cardinal <a href="/wiki/Gil_%C3%81lvarez_Carrillo_de_Albornoz" title="Gil Álvarez Carrillo de Albornoz">Albornoz</a>, who was charged with restoring the Church's power in Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Back in power for a short time, Cola was soon lynched by the populace, and Albornoz took possession of the city. In 1377, Rome became the seat of the papacy again under <a href="/wiki/Gregory_XI" class="mw-redirect" title="Gregory XI">Gregory XI</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The return of the pope to Rome in that year unleashed the <a href="/wiki/Western_Schism" title="Western Schism">Western Schism</a> (1377–1418), and for the next forty years, the city was affected by the divisions which rocked the Church.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Early_modern_history">Early modern history</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Roman_Renaissance" title="Roman Renaissance">Roman Renaissance</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Wolf-Dietrich-Klebeband_St%C3%A4dtebilder_G_123_III.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Wolf-Dietrich-Klebeband_St%C3%A4dtebilder_G_123_III.jpg/250px-Wolf-Dietrich-Klebeband_St%C3%A4dtebilder_G_123_III.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Wolf-Dietrich-Klebeband_St%C3%A4dtebilder_G_123_III.jpg/500px-Wolf-Dietrich-Klebeband_St%C3%A4dtebilder_G_123_III.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2000" data-file-height="1503"></a><figcaption>Almost 500 years old, this map of Rome by <a href="/wiki/Mario_Cartaro" title="Mario Cartaro">Mario Cartaro</a> (from 1575) shows the city's primary monuments.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:0_Castel_et_pont_Sant%27Angelo_(1).JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/0_Castel_et_pont_Sant%27Angelo_%281%29.JPG/250px-0_Castel_et_pont_Sant%27Angelo_%281%29.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/0_Castel_et_pont_Sant%27Angelo_%281%29.JPG/500px-0_Castel_et_pont_Sant%27Angelo_%281%29.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3852" data-file-height="2568"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Castel_Sant%27Angelo" title="Castel Sant'Angelo">Castel Sant'Angelo</a>, or Hadrian's Mausoleum, is a Roman monument built in 134 AD, radically altered in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and crowned with 16th and 17th-century statues.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fontana_della_Barcaccia_restaurata,_guardando_verso_Piazza_Mignanelli.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Fontana_della_Barcaccia_restaurata%2C_guardando_verso_Piazza_Mignanelli.jpg/250px-Fontana_della_Barcaccia_restaurata%2C_guardando_verso_Piazza_Mignanelli.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Fontana_della_Barcaccia_restaurata%2C_guardando_verso_Piazza_Mignanelli.jpg/500px-Fontana_della_Barcaccia_restaurata%2C_guardando_verso_Piazza_Mignanelli.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2560" data-file-height="1920"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Fontana_della_Barcaccia" title="Fontana della Barcaccia">Fontana della Barcaccia</a>, created by <a href="/wiki/Gian_Lorenzo_Bernini" title="Gian Lorenzo Bernini">Gian Lorenzo Bernini</a> in 1629</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1418, the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Constance" title="Council of Constance">Council of Constance</a> settled the <a href="/wiki/Western_Schism" title="Western Schism">Western Schism</a>, and a Roman pope, <a href="/wiki/Martin_V" class="mw-redirect" title="Martin V">Martin V</a>, was elected.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This brought to Rome a century of internal peace, which marked the beginning of the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The ruling popes until the first half of the 16th century, from <a href="/wiki/Nicholas_V" class="mw-redirect" title="Nicholas V">Nicholas V</a>, founder of the <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Library" title="Vatican Library">Vatican Library</a>, to <a href="/wiki/Pius_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Pius II">Pius II</a>, humanist and literate, from <a href="/wiki/Sixtus_IV" class="mw-redirect" title="Sixtus IV">Sixtus IV</a>, a warrior pope, to <a href="/wiki/Alexander_VI" class="mw-redirect" title="Alexander VI">Alexander VI</a>, immoral and <a href="/wiki/Nepotism" title="Nepotism">nepotist</a>, from <a href="/wiki/Julius_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Julius II">Julius II</a>, soldier and patron, to <a href="/wiki/Leo_X" class="mw-redirect" title="Leo X">Leo X</a>, who gave his name to this period ("the century of Leo X"), all devoted their energy to the greatness and the beauty of the Eternal City and to the patronage of the arts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During those years, the centre of the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Renaissance" title="Italian Renaissance">Italian Renaissance</a> moved to Rome from Florence. Majestic works, as the new <a href="/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Basilica" title="St. Peter's Basilica">Saint Peter's Basilica</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Sistine_Chapel" title="Sistine Chapel">Sistine Chapel</a> and <i><a href="/wiki/Ponte_Sisto" title="Ponte Sisto">Ponte Sisto</a></i> (the first bridge to be built across the <a href="/wiki/Tiber" title="Tiber">Tiber</a> since antiquity, although on Roman foundations) were created. To accomplish that, the Popes engaged the best artists of the time, including <a href="/wiki/Michelangelo" title="Michelangelo">Michelangelo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pietro_Perugino" title="Pietro Perugino">Perugino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Raphael" title="Raphael">Raphael</a>, <a href="/wiki/Domenico_Ghirlandaio" title="Domenico Ghirlandaio">Ghirlandaio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Luca_Signorelli" title="Luca Signorelli">Luca Signorelli</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sandro_Botticelli" title="Sandro Botticelli">Botticelli</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cosimo_Rosselli" title="Cosimo Rosselli">Cosimo Rosselli</a>.
</p><p>The period was also infamous for papal corruption, with many Popes fathering children, and engaging in <a href="/wiki/Nepotism" title="Nepotism">nepotism</a> and <a href="/wiki/Simony" title="Simony">simony</a>. The corruption of the Popes and the huge expenses for their building projects led, in part, to the <a href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Reformation</a> and, in turn, the <a href="/wiki/Counter-Reformation" title="Counter-Reformation">Counter-Reformation</a>. Under extravagant and rich popes, Rome was transformed into a centre of art, poetry, music, literature, education and culture. Rome became able to compete with other major European cities of the time in terms of wealth, grandeur, the arts, learning and architecture.
</p><p>The Renaissance period changed the face of Rome dramatically, with works like the <a href="/wiki/Piet%C3%A0_(Michelangelo)" title="Pietà (Michelangelo)">Pietà</a> by Michelangelo and the frescoes of the <a href="/wiki/Borgia_Apartments" title="Borgia Apartments">Borgia Apartments</a>. Rome reached the highest point of splendour under <a href="/wiki/Pope_Julius_II" title="Pope Julius II">Pope Julius II</a> (1503–1513) and his successors <a href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_X" title="Pope Leo X">Leo X</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pope_Clement_VII" title="Pope Clement VII">Clement VII</a>, both members of the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Medici" title="House of Medici">Medici family</a>.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Lingelbach,_Johannes_-_Carneval_in_Rom_-_c._1650-1651.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Lingelbach%2C_Johannes_-_Carneval_in_Rom_-_c._1650-1651.jpg/250px-Lingelbach%2C_Johannes_-_Carneval_in_Rom_-_c._1650-1651.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="209" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d8/Lingelbach%2C_Johannes_-_Carneval_in_Rom_-_c._1650-1651.jpg 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="418"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Carnival" title="Carnival">Carnival</a> in Rome, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 1650</span>, by <a href="/wiki/Johannes_Lingelbach" title="Johannes Lingelbach">Johannes Lingelbach</a></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:View_of_the_Piazza_Navona,_Rome_LACMA_49.17.3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/View_of_the_Piazza_Navona%2C_Rome_LACMA_49.17.3.jpg/250px-View_of_the_Piazza_Navona%2C_Rome_LACMA_49.17.3.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="107" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/View_of_the_Piazza_Navona%2C_Rome_LACMA_49.17.3.jpg/500px-View_of_the_Piazza_Navona%2C_Rome_LACMA_49.17.3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2083" data-file-height="894"></a><figcaption><i>A View of the Piazza Navona, Rome</i>, by <a href="/wiki/Hendrik_Frans_van_Lint" title="Hendrik Frans van Lint">Hendrik Frans van Lint</a>, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 1730</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>In this twenty-year period, Rome became one of the greatest centres of art in the world. The old St. Peter's Basilica built by Emperor <a href="/wiki/Constantine_the_Great" title="Constantine the Great">Constantine the Great</a><sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> (which by then was in a dilapidated state) was demolished and a new one begun. The city hosted artists like <a href="/wiki/Ridolfo_Ghirlandaio" title="Ridolfo Ghirlandaio">Ghirlandaio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pietro_Perugino" title="Pietro Perugino">Perugino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sandro_Botticelli" title="Sandro Botticelli">Botticelli</a> and <a href="/wiki/Donato_Bramante" title="Donato Bramante">Bramante</a>, who built the temple of <a href="/wiki/San_Pietro_in_Montorio" title="San Pietro in Montorio">San Pietro in Montorio</a> and planned a great project to renovate the <a href="/wiki/Apostolic_Palace" title="Apostolic Palace">Vatican</a>. Raphael, who in Rome became one of the most famous painters of Italy, created frescoes in the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Farnesina" title="Villa Farnesina">Villa Farnesina</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Raphael_Rooms" title="Raphael Rooms">Raphael's Rooms</a>, plus many other famous paintings. Michelangelo started the decoration of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and executed the famous statue of the <a href="/wiki/Moses" title="Moses">Moses</a> for the tomb of Julius II.
</p><p>Its economy was rich, with the presence of several Tuscan bankers, including <a href="/wiki/Agostino_Chigi" title="Agostino Chigi">Agostino Chigi</a>, who was a friend of Raphael and a patron of arts. Before his early death, Raphael also promoted for the first time the preservation of the ancient ruins. The <a href="/wiki/War_of_the_League_of_Cognac" title="War of the League of Cognac">War of the League of Cognac</a> caused the first plunder of the city in more than five hundred years since <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(1084)" title="Sack of Rome (1084)">the previous sack</a>; in 1527, the <a href="/wiki/Landsknecht" title="Landsknecht">Landsknechts</a> of Emperor <a href="/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor" title="Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor">Charles V</a> <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(1527)" title="Sack of Rome (1527)">sacked the city</a>, bringing an abrupt end to the golden age of the Renaissance in Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Beginning with the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Trent" title="Council of Trent">Council of Trent</a> in 1545, the Church began the Counter-Reformation in response to the Reformation, a large-scale questioning of the Church's authority on spiritual matters and governmental affairs. This loss of confidence led to major shifts of power away from the Church.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Under the popes from <a href="/wiki/Pius_IV" class="mw-redirect" title="Pius IV">Pius IV</a> to <a href="/wiki/Sixtus_V" class="mw-redirect" title="Sixtus V">Sixtus V</a>, Rome became the centre of a reformed Catholicism and saw the building of new monuments which celebrated the papacy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The popes and cardinals of the 17th and early 18th centuries continued the movement by having the city's landscape enriched with baroque buildings.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523_77-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>This was another nepotistic age; the new aristocratic families (<a href="/wiki/Barberini_family" title="Barberini family">Barberini</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pamphili_family" title="Pamphili family">Pamphili</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chigi_family" title="Chigi family">Chigi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rospigliosi_family" title="Rospigliosi family">Rospigliosi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Altieri_family" title="Altieri family">Altieri</a>, <a href="/wiki/Odescalchi_family" class="mw-redirect" title="Odescalchi family">Odescalchi</a>) were protected by their respective popes, who built huge baroque buildings for their relatives.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523_77-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192523-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the <a href="/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment" title="Age of Enlightenment">Age of Enlightenment</a>, new ideas reached the Eternal City, where the papacy supported archaeological studies and improved the people's welfare.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> But not everything went well for the Church during the Counter-Reformation. There were setbacks in the attempts to assert the Church's power, a notable example being in 1773 when Pope Clement XIV was forced by secular powers to have the <a href="/wiki/Suppression_of_the_Society_of_Jesus" title="Suppression of the Society of Jesus">Jesuit order suppressed</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522_75-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBertarelli192522-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Late_modern_and_contemporary">Late modern and contemporary</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Breccia_di_Porta_Pia_Ademollo.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Breccia_di_Porta_Pia_Ademollo.jpg/250px-Breccia_di_Porta_Pia_Ademollo.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="132" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Breccia_di_Porta_Pia_Ademollo.jpg/500px-Breccia_di_Porta_Pia_Ademollo.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2452" data-file-height="1298"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Bersaglieri" title="Bersaglieri">Bersaglieri</a> troops breaching the <a href="/wiki/Aurelian_Walls" title="Aurelian Walls">Aurelian Walls</a> at <a href="/wiki/Porta_Pia" title="Porta Pia">Porta Pia</a> during the <i><a href="/wiki/Capture_of_Rome" title="Capture of Rome">Capture of Rome</a></i> (1870), the final event of the <a href="/wiki/Italian_unification" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian unification">Italian unification</a>. Painting by <a href="/wiki/Carlo_Ademollo" title="Carlo Ademollo">Carlo Ademollo</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The rule of the Popes was interrupted by the short-lived <a href="/wiki/Roman_Republic_(18th_century)" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Republic (18th century)">Roman Republic</a> (1798–1800), which was established under the influence of the <a href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Papal_States" title="Papal States">Papal States</a> were restored in June 1800, but during <a href="/wiki/Napoleon" title="Napoleon">Napoleon</a>'s reign Rome was <a href="/wiki/Rome_(department)" title="Rome (department)">annexed as a <i>Département</i></a> of the <a href="/wiki/First_French_Empire" title="First French Empire">French Empire</a>: first as <i>Département du Tibre</i> (1809–1810) and then as <i>Département Rome</i> (1810–1814). After the fall of Napoleon, the Papal States were reconstituted by a decision of the <a href="/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna" title="Congress of Vienna">Congress of Vienna</a> of 1814.
</p><p>In 1849, <a href="/wiki/Roman_Republic_(19th_century)" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Republic (19th century)">a second Roman Republic</a> was proclaimed during a year of <a href="/wiki/Revolutions_in_1848" class="mw-redirect" title="Revolutions in 1848">revolutions in 1848</a>. Two of the most influential figures of the <a href="/wiki/Italian_unification" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian unification">Italian unification</a>, <a href="/wiki/Giuseppe_Mazzini" title="Giuseppe Mazzini">Giuseppe Mazzini</a> and <a href="/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi" title="Giuseppe Garibaldi">Giuseppe Garibaldi</a>, fought for the short-lived republic.
</p><p>Rome then became the focus of hopes of Italian reunification after the rest of Italy was united as the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy" title="Kingdom of Italy">Kingdom of Italy</a> in 1861 with the temporary capital in <a href="/wiki/Florence" title="Florence">Florence</a>. That year Rome was declared the capital of Italy even though it was still under the Pope's control. During the 1860s, the last vestiges of the Papal States were under French protection thanks to the foreign policy of <a href="/wiki/Napoleon_III" title="Napoleon III">Napoleon III</a>. French troops were stationed in the region under Papal control. In 1870 the French troops were withdrawn due to the outbreak of the <a href="/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War" title="Franco-Prussian War">Franco-Prussian War</a>. Italian troops were able to <a href="/wiki/Capture_of_Rome" title="Capture of Rome">capture Rome</a> entering the city through a breach near <a href="/wiki/Porta_Pia" title="Porta Pia">Porta Pia</a>. <a href="/wiki/Pope_Pius_IX" title="Pope Pius IX">Pope Pius IX</a> declared himself a <a href="/wiki/Prisoner_in_the_Vatican" title="Prisoner in the Vatican">prisoner in the Vatican</a>. In 1871 the capital of Italy was moved from Florence to Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 1870 the population of the city was 212,000, all of whom lived with the area circumscribed by the ancient city, and in 1920, the population was 660,000. A significant portion lived outside the walls in the north and across the Tiber in the Vatican area.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Bombardamento_di_Roma.gif" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Bombardamento_di_Roma.gif/250px-Bombardamento_di_Roma.gif" decoding="async" width="250" height="179" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Bombardamento_di_Roma.gif/500px-Bombardamento_di_Roma.gif 2x" data-file-width="5010" data-file-height="3594"></a><figcaption>Bombardment of Rome by <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allied</a> planes, 1943</figcaption></figure>
<p>Soon after World War I in late 1922 Rome witnessed the rise of <a href="/wiki/Italian_Fascism" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian Fascism">Italian Fascism</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Benito_Mussolini" title="Benito Mussolini">Benito Mussolini</a>, who led a <a href="/wiki/March_on_Rome" title="March on Rome">march on the city</a>. He did away with democracy by 1926, eventually declaring a new <a href="/wiki/Imperial_Italy_(fascist)" class="mw-redirect" title="Imperial Italy (fascist)">Italian Empire</a> and allying Italy with <a href="/wiki/Nazi_Germany" title="Nazi Germany">Nazi Germany</a> in 1938. Mussolini demolished fairly large parts of the city centre in order to build wide avenues and squares which were supposed to celebrate the fascist regime and the resurgence and glorification of classical Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The interwar period saw a rapid growth in the city's population which surpassed one million inhabitants soon after 1930. During World War II, due to the art treasuries and the presence of the Vatican, Rome largely escaped the tragic destiny of other European cities. However, on 19 July 1943, the <a href="/wiki/Quartiere_San_Lorenzo" class="mw-redirect" title="Quartiere San Lorenzo">San Lorenzo district</a> was <a href="/wiki/Bombing_of_Rome_in_World_War_II" title="Bombing of Rome in World War II">subject to Allied bombing raids</a>, resulting in about 3,000 fatalities and 11,000 injuries, of whom another 1,500 died.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mussolini <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Fascist_regime_in_Italy" title="Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy">was arrested on 25 July 1943</a>. On the date of the <a href="/wiki/Armistice_of_Cassibile" title="Armistice of Cassibile">Italian Armistice</a> 8 September 1943 the city was occupied by the Germans. Allied bombing raids continued throughout 1943 and extended into 1944. Rome was liberated on 4 June 1944.
</p><p>Rome developed greatly after the war as part of the "<a href="/wiki/Italian_economic_miracle" title="Italian economic miracle">Italian economic miracle</a>" of post-war reconstruction and modernisation in the 1950s and early 1960s. During this period, the years of <i>la dolce vita</i> ("the sweet life"), Rome became a fashionable city, with popular classic films such as <i><a href="/wiki/Ben-Hur_(1959_film)" title="Ben-Hur (1959 film)">Ben Hur</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Quo_Vadis_(1951_film)" title="Quo Vadis (1951 film)">Quo Vadis</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Roman_Holiday" title="Roman Holiday">Roman Holiday</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/La_Dolce_Vita" title="La Dolce Vita">La Dolce Vita</a></i> filmed in the city's iconic <a href="/wiki/Cinecitt%C3%A0" title="Cinecittà">Cinecittà Studios</a>. The rising trend in population growth continued until the mid-1980s when the <i>comune</i> had more than 2.8 million residents. After this, the population declined slowly as people began to move to nearby suburbs.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Geography">Geography</h2></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Location">Location</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rome,_Italy_ESA24383157.jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Rome%2C_Italy_ESA24383157.jpeg/250px-Rome%2C_Italy_ESA24383157.jpeg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Rome%2C_Italy_ESA24383157.jpeg/500px-Rome%2C_Italy_ESA24383157.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="4724" data-file-height="3149"></a><figcaption>Satellite image of Rome</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is in the <a href="/wiki/Lazio" title="Lazio">Lazio</a> region of <a href="/wiki/Central_Italy" title="Central Italy">central Italy</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Tiber" title="Tiber">Tiber</a> (<a href="/wiki/Italian_language" title="Italian language">Italian</a>: <i lang="it">Tevere</i>) river. The original settlement developed on hills that faced onto a ford beside the <a href="/wiki/Tiber_Island" title="Tiber Island">Tiber Island</a>, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was built on seven hills: the <a href="/wiki/Aventine_Hill" title="Aventine Hill">Aventine Hill</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Caelian_Hill" title="Caelian Hill">Caelian Hill</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Capitoline_Hill" title="Capitoline Hill">Capitoline Hill</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Esquiline_Hill" title="Esquiline Hill">Esquiline Hill</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Palatine_Hill" title="Palatine Hill">Palatine Hill</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Hill" title="Quirinal Hill">Quirinal Hill</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Viminal_Hill" title="Viminal Hill">Viminal Hill</a>. Modern Rome is also crossed by another river, the <a href="/wiki/Aniene" title="Aniene">Aniene</a>, which flows into the Tiber north of the historic centre.
</p><p>Although the city centre is about 24 km (15 mi) inland from the <a href="/wiki/Tyrrhenian_Sea" title="Tyrrhenian Sea">Tyrrhenian Sea</a>, the city territory extends to the shore, where the south-western district of <a href="/wiki/Ostia_(Rome)" title="Ostia (Rome)">Ostia</a> is located. The altitude of the central part of Rome ranges from 13 m (43 ft) <a href="/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level" class="mw-redirect" title="Above mean sea level">above sea level</a> (at the base of the <a href="/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome" title="Pantheon, Rome">Pantheon</a>) to 139 m (456 ft) <a href="/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level" class="mw-redirect" title="Above mean sea level">above sea level</a> (the peak of <a href="/wiki/Monte_Mario" title="Monte Mario">Monte Mario</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <i>Comune</i> of Rome covers an overall area of about 1,285 km<sup>2</sup> (496 sq mi), including many green areas.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Parks_and_gardens">Parks and gardens</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_parks_and_gardens_in_Rome" title="List of parks and gardens in Rome">List of parks and gardens in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rome-VillaBorghese-TempleEsculape.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Rome-VillaBorghese-TempleEsculape.jpg/250px-Rome-VillaBorghese-TempleEsculape.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Rome-VillaBorghese-TempleEsculape.jpg/500px-Rome-VillaBorghese-TempleEsculape.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3176" data-file-height="2382"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Temple_of_Aesculapius_(Villa_Borghese)" title="Temple of Aesculapius (Villa Borghese)">Temple of Aesculapius</a>, in the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Borghese_gardens" title="Villa Borghese gardens">Villa Borghese gardens</a></figcaption></figure>
