<p>Public parks and nature reserves cover a large area in Rome, and the city has one of the largest areas of green space among European capitals.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The most notable part of this green space is represented by the large number of villas and landscaped gardens created by the Italian aristocracy. While most of the parks surrounding the villas were destroyed during the building boom of the late 19th century, some of them remain. The most notable of these are the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Borghese_gardens" title="Villa Borghese gardens">Villa Borghese</a>, <a href="/wiki/Villa_Ada" title="Villa Ada">Villa Ada</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Villa_Doria_Pamphili" title="Villa Doria Pamphili">Villa Doria Pamphili</a>. Villa Doria Pamphili is west of the Gianicolo hill, comprising some 1.8 km<sup>2</sup> (0.7 <a href="/wiki/Square_mile" title="Square mile">sq mi</a>). The <a href="/wiki/Villa_Sciarra_(Rome)" title="Villa Sciarra (Rome)">Villa Sciarra</a> is on the hill, with playgrounds for children and shaded walking areas. In the nearby area of Trastevere, the <a href="/wiki/Orto_Botanico_dell%27Universit%C3%A0_di_Roma_%22La_Sapienza%22" title="Orto Botanico dell'Università di Roma "La Sapienza"">Orto Botanico</a> (Botanical Garden) is a cool and shady green space. The old Roman hippodrome (Circus Maximus) is another large green space: it has few trees but is overlooked by the Palatine and the Rose Garden ('roseto comunale'). Nearby is the lush <a href="/wiki/Villa_Celimontana" title="Villa Celimontana">Villa Celimontana</a>, close to the gardens surrounding the Baths of Caracalla. The Villa Borghese garden is the best known large green space in Rome, with famous art galleries among its shaded walks. Overlooking <a href="/wiki/Piazza_del_Popolo" title="Piazza del Popolo">Piazza del Popolo</a> and the Spanish Steps are the gardens of <a href="/wiki/Pincio" class="mw-redirect" title="Pincio">Pincio</a> and <a href="/wiki/Villa_Medici" title="Villa Medici">Villa Medici</a>. There is also a notable pine wood at <a href="/wiki/Castelfusano" title="Castelfusano">Castelfusano</a>, near Ostia. Rome also has a number of regional parks of much more recent origin, including the <a href="/wiki/Pineto_Regional_Park" title="Pineto Regional Park">Pineto Regional Park</a> and the Appian Way Regional Park. There are also nature reserves at Marcigliana and at Tenuta di Castelporziano.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Climate">Climate</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Climate_of_Rome" title="Climate of Rome">Climate of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Doria_Pamphili_6376.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Doria_Pamphili_6376.jpg/250px-Doria_Pamphili_6376.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Doria_Pamphili_6376.jpg/500px-Doria_Pamphili_6376.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1800" data-file-height="1200"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Stone_pine" title="Stone pine">Stone pines</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Doria_Pamphili" title="Villa Doria Pamphili">Villa Doria Pamphili</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome has a <a href="/wiki/Hot-summer_Mediterranean_climate" class="mw-redirect" title="Hot-summer Mediterranean climate">Mediterranean climate</a> (<a href="/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification" title="Köppen climate classification">Köppen climate classification</a>: <i>Csa</i>),<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> with hot, dry summers and mild, humid winters.
</p><p>Its average annual temperature is above 21 °C (70 °F) during the day and 9 °C (48 °F) at night. In the coldest month, January, the average temperature is 12.6 °C (54.7 °F) during the day and 2.1 °C (35.8 °F) at night. In the warmest month, August, the average temperature is 31.7 °C (89.1 °F) during the day and 17.3 °C (63.1 °F) at night.
</p><p>December, January and February are the coldest months, with a daily mean temperature of approximately 8 °C (46 °F). Temperatures during these months generally vary between 10 and 15 °C (50 and 59 °F) during the day and between 3 and 5 °C (37 and 41 °F) at night, with colder or warmer spells occurring frequently. Snowfall is rare but not unheard of, with light snow or flurries occurring on some winters, generally without accumulation, and major snowfalls on a very rare occurrence (the most recent ones were in 2018, 2012 and 1986).<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The average <a href="/wiki/Relative_humidity" class="mw-redirect" title="Relative humidity">relative humidity</a> is 75%, varying from 72% in July to 77% in November. Sea temperatures vary from a low of 13.9 °C (57.0 °F) in February to a high of 25.0 °C (77.0 °F) in August.<sup id="cite_ref-seatemperature.org2_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-seatemperature.org2-87"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The highest temperature ever recorded in Rome was 42.9 °C (109.2 °F) on 18 July 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

<p>By 550 BC, Rome was the second largest city in Italy after only Taras (modern <a href="/wiki/Taranto" title="Taranto">Taranto</a>) on the <a href="/wiki/Salento_Peninsula" class="mw-redirect" title="Salento Peninsula">Salento Peninsula</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It had an area of about 285 ha (700 acres) and an estimated population of 35,000. Other sources suggest the population was just under 100,000 from 600 to 500 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> When the Republic was founded in 509 BC the census recorded a population of 130,000.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The republic included the city itself and the immediate surroundings. Other sources suggest a population of 150,000 in 500 BC. It surpassed 300,000 by 150 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The size of the city at the time of the Emperor <a href="/wiki/Augustus" title="Augustus">Augustus</a> is a matter of speculation, with estimates based on grain distribution, grain imports, aqueduct capacity, city limits, population density, census reports, and assumptions about the number of unreported women, children and slaves providing a very wide range. Glenn Storey estimates 450,000 people, <a href="/wiki/Whitney_Oates" class="mw-redirect" title="Whitney Oates">Whitney Oates</a> estimates 1.2 million, Neville Morely provides a rough estimate of 800,000 and excludes earlier suggestions of 2 million.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Estimates of the city's population towards and after the end of the Roman empire also vary. A.H.M. Jones estimated the population at 650,000 in the mid-fifth century. The damage caused by the sackings may have been overestimated. The population had already started to decline from the late fourth century onward, although around the middle of the fifth century it seems that Rome continued to be the most populous city of the two parts of the Empire.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to Krautheimer it was still close to 800,000 in 400 AD; had declined to 500,000 by 452, and dwindled to perhaps 100,000 in 500 AD. After the Gothic Wars, 535–552, the population may have dwindled temporarily to 30,000. During the pontificate of <a href="/wiki/Pope_Gregory_I" title="Pope Gregory I">Pope Gregory I</a> (590–604), it may have reached 90,000, augmented by refugees.<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Lancon estimates 500,000 based on the number of 'incisi' enrolled as eligible to receive bread, oil and wine rations; the number fell to 120,000 in the <a href="/w/index.php?title=Reform_of_419&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Reform of 419 (page does not exist)">reform of 419</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Neil Christie, citing free rations for the poorest, estimated 500,000 in the mid-fifth century and still a quarter of a million at the end of the century.<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Novel 36 of Emperor <a href="/wiki/Valentinian_III" title="Valentinian III">Valentinian III</a> records 3.629 million pounds of pork to be distributed to the needy at 5 lbs. per month for the five winter months, sufficient for 145,000 recipients. This has been used to suggest a population of just under 500,000. Supplies of grain remained steady until the seizure of the remaining provinces of North Africa in 439 by the <a href="/wiki/Vandals" title="Vandals">Vandals</a>, and may have continued to some degree afterwards for a while. The city's population declined to less than 50,000 people in the <a href="/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages" title="Early Middle Ages">Early Middle Ages</a> from 700 onward. It continued to stagnate or shrink until the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>When the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy" title="Kingdom of Italy">Kingdom of Italy</a> annexed Rome in 1870, the city had a population of about 225,000. Less than half the city within the walls was built up in 1881 when the population recorded was 275,000. This increased to 600,000 by the eve of World War I. The <a href="/wiki/Fascism" title="Fascism">Fascist</a> regime of Mussolini tried to block an excessive demographic rise of the city but failed to prevent it from reaching one million people by the early 1930s.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2014)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (March 2014)">clarification needed</span></a></i>]</sup> Population growth continued after the Second World War, helped by a post-war economic boom. A construction boom also created many suburbs during the 1950s and 1960s.
</p><p>In mid-2010, there were 2,754,440 residents in the city proper, while some 4.2 million people lived in the greater Rome area (which can be approximately identified with its administrative metropolitan city, with a population density of about 800 inhabitants/km<sup>2</sup> stretching over more than 5,000 km<sup>2</sup> (1,900 sq mi)). Minors (children ages 18 and younger) totalled 17.00% of the population compared to pensioners who number 20.76%. This compares with the Italian average of 18.06% (minors) and 19.94% (pensioners). The average age of a Roman resident is 43 compared to the Italian average of 42. In the five years between 2002 and 2007, the population of Rome grew by 6.54%, while Italy as a whole grew by 3.56%.<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The current<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="The time period mentioned near this tag is ambiguous. (August 2017)">when?</span></a></i>]</sup> birth rate of Rome is 9.10 births per 1,000 inhabitants compared to the Italian average of 9.45 births.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup>
</p><p>The urban area of Rome extends beyond the administrative city limits with a population of around 3.9 million.<sup id="cite_ref-World_Urban_Areas_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-World_Urban_Areas-112"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Between 3.2 and 4.2 million people live in the <a href="/wiki/Rome_metropolitan_area" title="Rome metropolitan area">Rome metropolitan area</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Origin_groups">Origin groups</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Piazza_Santa_Maria_Maggiore_din_Roma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Piazza_Santa_Maria_Maggiore_din_Roma.jpg/250px-Piazza_Santa_Maria_Maggiore_din_Roma.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Piazza_Santa_Maria_Maggiore_din_Roma.jpg/500px-Piazza_Santa_Maria_Maggiore_din_Roma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3000"></a><figcaption>Piazza Santa Maria Maggiore, in the <a href="/wiki/Esquilino_(rione_of_Rome)" title="Esquilino (rione of Rome)">Esquilino</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Rioni_of_Rome" title="Rioni of Rome">rione</a></i></figcaption></figure>
<p>According to the 2011 statistics conducted by ISTAT,<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> approximately 9.5% of the population consists of non-Italians. About half of the immigrant population consists of those of various other European origins (chiefly Romanian, Polish, Ukrainian, and Albanian) numbering a combined total of 131,118 or 4.7% of the population. The remaining 4.8% are those with non-European origins, chiefly <a href="/wiki/Filipinos" title="Filipinos">Filipinos</a> (26,933), Bangladeshis (12,154), and Chinese (10,283).
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Esquilino_(rione_of_Rome)" title="Esquilino (rione of Rome)">Esquilino</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Rioni_of_Rome" title="Rioni of Rome">rione</a></i>, off <a href="/wiki/Termini_Station_(Rome)" class="mw-redirect" title="Termini Station (Rome)">Termini Railway Station</a>, has evolved into a largely immigrant neighbourhood. It is perceived as Rome's Chinatown. Immigrants from more than a hundred different countries reside there. A commercial district, Esquilino contains restaurants featuring many kinds of international cuisine. There are wholesale clothes shops. Of the 1,300 or so commercial premises operating in the district 800 are Chinese-owned; around 300 are run by immigrants from other countries around the world; 200 are owned by Italians.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Language">Language</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Roman_dialect" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman dialect">Roman dialect</a> and <a href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Nove-bone.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Nove-bone.jpg/250px-Nove-bone.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Nove-bone.jpg/500px-Nove-bone.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1536"></a><figcaption>Advertisement in <a href="/wiki/Romanesco_dialect" title="Romanesco dialect">Romanesco dialect</a> at a subway station in Rome</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome's historic contribution to language in a worldwide sense is extensive. Through the process of <a href="/wiki/Romanization_(cultural)" title="Romanization (cultural)">Romanization</a>, the peoples of Italy, <a href="/wiki/Gallia" class="mw-redirect" title="Gallia">Gallia</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian Peninsula</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dacia" title="Dacia">Dacia</a> developed languages which derive directly from Latin and were adopted in large areas of the world, all through cultural influence, colonisation and migration. Moreover, also modern English, because of the <a href="/wiki/Norman_Conquest" title="Norman Conquest">Norman Conquest</a>, borrowed a large percentage of its vocabulary from the Latin language. The <a href="/wiki/Latin_alphabet" title="Latin alphabet">Roman or Latin alphabet</a> is the most widely used writing system in the world used by the greatest number of languages.<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The medieval <a href="/wiki/Roman_dialect" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman dialect">Roman dialect</a> belonged to the southern family of Italian dialects, and was thus much closer to the <a href="/wiki/Neapolitan_language" title="Neapolitan language">Neapolitan language</a> than to the Florentine.<sup id="cite_ref-sie_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sie-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A typical example of Romanesco of that period is <i><a href="/w/index.php?title=Cronica_dell%27Anonimo_Romano&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Cronica dell'Anonimo Romano (page does not exist)">Vita di Cola di Rienzo</a><span class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;"> [<a href="https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronica_dell%27Anonimo_Romano" class="extiw" title="it:Cronica dell'Anonimo Romano">it</a>]</span></i> ("Life of <a href="/wiki/Cola_di_Rienzo" title="Cola di Rienzo">Cola di Rienzo</a>"), written by an anonymous Roman during the 14th century.<sup id="cite_ref-sie_122-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sie-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Starting with the 16th century, the Roman dialect underwent a stronger and stronger influence from the <a href="/wiki/Tuscan_dialect" class="mw-redirect" title="Tuscan dialect">Tuscan dialect</a> (from which modern Italian derives) starting with the reigns of the two <a href="/wiki/House_of_Medici" title="House of Medici">Medici</a> popes (<a href="/wiki/Leo_X" class="mw-redirect" title="Leo X">Leo X</a> and <a href="/wiki/Clement_VII" class="mw-redirect" title="Clement VII">Clement VII</a>) and with the <a href="/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(1527)" title="Sack of Rome (1527)">Sack of Rome in 1527</a>, two events which provoked a large immigration from <a href="/wiki/Tuscany" title="Tuscany">Tuscany</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-dia_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-dia-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Therefore, current Romanesco has grammar and roots that are rather different from other dialects in Central Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-dia_125-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-dia-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Religion">Religion</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_Rome" title="Religion in Rome">Religion in Rome</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Vatican_City" title="Vatican City">Vatican City</a> and <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Rome" title="History of the Jews in Rome">History of the Jews in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:San_Giovanni_in_Laterano_2021.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/San_Giovanni_in_Laterano_2021.jpg/250px-San_Giovanni_in_Laterano_2021.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/San_Giovanni_in_Laterano_2021.jpg/500px-San_Giovanni_in_Laterano_2021.jpg 2x" data-file-width="8874" data-file-height="6651"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Archbasilica_of_Saint_John_Lateran" title="Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran">Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran</a>, Rome's Cathedral, built in 324, and partly rebuilt between 1660 and 1734</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Santa_Maria_Maggiore_Front.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Santa_Maria_Maggiore_Front.JPG/250px-Santa_Maria_Maggiore_Front.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="221" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Santa_Maria_Maggiore_Front.JPG/500px-Santa_Maria_Maggiore_Front.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2968" data-file-height="2623"></a><figcaption>One of the <a href="/wiki/Seven_Pilgrim_Churches_of_Rome" title="Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome">Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome</a>, <a href="/wiki/Santa_Maria_Maggiore" title="Santa Maria Maggiore">Santa Maria Maggiore</a> is the city's largest <a href="/wiki/Catholic_Marian_church_buildings" title="Catholic Marian church buildings">Catholic Marian church</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Celebrazione_del_2777_Natale_di_Roma_-_Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile_2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Celebrazione_del_2777_Natale_di_Roma_-_Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile_2.jpg/250px-Celebrazione_del_2777_Natale_di_Roma_-_Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile_2.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="122" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Celebrazione_del_2777_Natale_di_Roma_-_Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile_2.jpg/500px-Celebrazione_del_2777_Natale_di_Roma_-_Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile_2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1080" data-file-height="525"></a><figcaption>Celebration of the 2777th <a href="/wiki/Natale_di_Roma" title="Natale di Roma">Natale di Roma</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Circus_Maximus" title="Circus Maximus">Circus Maximus</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Much like the rest of Italy, Rome is predominantly <a href="/wiki/Christianity" title="Christianity">Christian</a>, and the city has been an important centre of religion and <a href="/wiki/Christian_pilgrimage" title="Christian pilgrimage">pilgrimage</a> for centuries, the base of the ancient Roman religion with the <a href="/wiki/Pontifex_Maximus" class="mw-redirect" title="Pontifex Maximus">pontifex maximus</a> and later the seat of the <a href="/wiki/Holy_See" title="Holy See">Vatican</a> and the pope. Before the arrival of the Christians in Rome, the <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_ancient_Rome" title="Religion in ancient Rome">Religio Romana</a> (literally, the "Roman Religion") was the major religion of the city in classical antiquity. The first gods held sacred by the Romans were <a href="/wiki/Jupiter_(mythology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jupiter (mythology)">Jupiter</a>, the Most High, and <a href="/wiki/Mars_(mythology)" title="Mars (mythology)">Mars</a>, the god of war, and father of Rome's twin founders, <a href="/wiki/Romulus_and_Remus" title="Romulus and Remus">Romulus and Remus</a>, according to tradition. Other deities such as <a href="/wiki/Vesta_(mythology)" title="Vesta (mythology)">Vesta</a> and <a href="/wiki/Minerva" title="Minerva">Minerva</a> were honoured. Rome was also the base of several mystery cults, such as <a href="/wiki/Mithraic_Mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Mithraic Mysteries">Mithraism</a>. Later, after <a href="/wiki/Saint_Peter" title="Saint Peter">St Peter</a> and <a href="/wiki/Paul_the_Apostle" title="Paul the Apostle">St Paul</a> were martyred in the city, and the first Christians began to arrive, Rome became Christian, and the <a href="/wiki/Old_St._Peter%27s_Basilica" title="Old St. Peter's Basilica">Old St. Peter's Basilica</a> was constructed in 313 AD. Despite some interruptions (such as the <a href="/wiki/Avignon_Papacy" title="Avignon Papacy">Avignon papacy</a>), Rome has for centuries been the home of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholic Church">Roman Catholic Church</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Pope" title="Pope">Bishop of Rome</a>, otherwise known as the Pope.
</p><p>Despite the fact that Rome is home to the <a href="/wiki/Vatican_City" title="Vatican City">Vatican City</a> and St. Peter's Basilica, Rome's cathedral is the <a href="/wiki/Archbasilica_of_Saint_John_Lateran" title="Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran">Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran</a>, in the south-east of the city centre. There are around 900 churches in Rome in total. Aside from the cathedral itself, some others of note include the <a href="/wiki/Basilica_di_Santa_Maria_Maggiore" class="mw-redirect" title="Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore">Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint_Paul_Outside_the_Walls" title="Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls">Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Basilica_di_San_Clemente" class="mw-redirect" title="Basilica di San Clemente">Basilica di San Clemente</a>, <a href="/wiki/San_Carlo_alle_Quattro_Fontane" title="San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane">San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_the_Gesu" class="mw-redirect" title="Church of the Gesu">Church of the Gesù</a>. There are also the ancient <a href="/wiki/Catacombs_of_Rome" title="Catacombs of Rome">Catacombs of Rome</a> underneath the city. Numerous highly important religious educational institutions are also in Rome, such as the <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Lateran_University" title="Pontifical Lateran University">Pontifical Lateran University</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Biblical_Institute" title="Pontifical Biblical Institute">Pontifical Biblical Institute</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Gregorian_University" title="Pontifical Gregorian University">Pontifical Gregorian University</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Oriental_Institute" title="Pontifical Oriental Institute">Pontifical Oriental Institute</a>.
</p><p>Since the end of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Roman Republic</a>, Rome is also the centre of an important <a href="/wiki/Jewish" class="mw-redirect" title="Jewish">Jewish</a> community,<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which was once based in <a href="/wiki/Trastevere" title="Trastevere">Trastevere</a>, and later in the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Ghetto" title="Roman Ghetto">Roman Ghetto</a>. There lies also the major synagogue in Rome, the <i><a href="/wiki/Great_Synagogue_of_Rome" title="Great Synagogue of Rome">Tempio Maggiore</a></i>.
</p><p>The territory of <a href="/wiki/Vatican_City" title="Vatican City">Vatican City</a> is part of the <i>Mons Vaticanus</i> (<a href="/wiki/Vatican_Hill" title="Vatican Hill">Vatican Hill</a>), and of the adjacent former Vatican Fields, where <a href="/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Basilica" title="St. Peter's Basilica">St. Peter's Basilica</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Apostolic_Palace" title="Apostolic Palace">Apostolic Palace</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Sistine_Chapel" title="Sistine Chapel">Sistine Chapel</a>, and museums were built, along with various other buildings. The area was part of the Roman <a href="/wiki/Rione" class="mw-redirect" title="Rione">rione</a> of <a href="/wiki/Borgo_(rione_of_Rome)" title="Borgo (rione of Rome)">Borgo</a> until 1929. Being separated from the city on the west bank of the <a href="/wiki/Tiber" title="Tiber">Tiber</a>, the area was a suburb that was protected by being included within the walls of <a href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_IV" title="Pope Leo IV">Leo IV</a>, later expanded by the current fortification walls of <a href="/wiki/Pope_Paul_III" title="Pope Paul III">Paul III</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pope_Pius_IV" title="Pope Pius IV">Pius IV</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pope_Urban_VIII" title="Pope Urban VIII">Urban VIII</a>. When the <a href="/wiki/Lateran_Treaty" title="Lateran Treaty">Lateran Treaty</a> of 1929 that created the Vatican state was being prepared, the boundaries of the proposed territory were influenced by the fact that much of it was all but enclosed by this loop.
</p><p>Rome has been a major <a href="/wiki/Christian_pilgrimage" title="Christian pilgrimage">Christian pilgrimage</a> site since the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</a>. People from all over the <a href="/wiki/Christian_world" class="mw-redirect" title="Christian world">Christian world</a> visit Vatican City, within the city of Rome, the seat of the papacy. The city became a major <a href="/wiki/Pilgrimage" title="Pilgrimage">pilgrimage</a> site during the Middle Ages. Apart from brief periods as an independent city during the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</a>, Rome kept its status as Papal capital and holy city for centuries, even when the Papacy <a href="/wiki/Avignon_papacy" class="mw-redirect" title="Avignon papacy">briefly relocated</a> to <a href="/wiki/Avignon" title="Avignon">Avignon</a> (1309–1377). Catholics believe that the Vatican is the last resting place of St. Peter. Pilgrimages to Rome can involve visits to many sites, both within Vatican City and in Italian territory. A popular stopping point is the <a href="/wiki/Scala_sancta" class="mw-redirect" title="Scala sancta">Pilate's stairs</a>: these are, according to the Christian tradition, the steps that led up to the <a href="/wiki/Praetorium" title="Praetorium">praetorium</a> of <a href="/wiki/Pontius_Pilate" title="Pontius Pilate">Pontius Pilate</a> in <a href="/wiki/Jerusalem" title="Jerusalem">Jerusalem</a>, which <a href="/wiki/Jesus_Christ" class="mw-redirect" title="Jesus Christ">Jesus Christ</a> stood on during his <a href="/wiki/Passion_(Christianity)" class="mw-redirect" title="Passion (Christianity)">Passion</a> on his way to trial.<sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In addition, Rome hosts multiple <a href="/wiki/Buddhist" class="mw-redirect" title="Buddhist">Buddhist</a><sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> temples, and a variety of <a href="/wiki/Reconstructionist_Roman_religion" title="Reconstructionist Roman religion">Roman modern pagan</a> temples <sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>125<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> held by the <a href="/wiki/Pietas_Comunit%C3%A0_Gentile" title="Pietas Comunità Gentile">Associazione Tradizionale Pietas</a> which every year takes part in the religious festivities of the <a href="/wiki/Natale_di_Roma" title="Natale di Roma">Natale di Roma</a>, historically known as <i>Dies Romana</i> and also referred to as Romaia, the festival linked to the <a href="/wiki/Foundation_of_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Foundation of Rome">foundation of Rome</a>, celebrated on 21 April.<sup id="cite_ref-Plutarch12_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Plutarch12-130"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to <a href="/wiki/Legend" title="Legend">legend</a>, <a href="/wiki/Romulus" title="Romulus">Romulus</a> is said to have founded the city of Rome on 21 April, <a href="/wiki/753_BC" class="mw-redirect" title="753 BC">753 BC</a>. From this date, the Roman chronology derived its system, known by the <a href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</a> phrase <i><a href="/wiki/Ab_Urbe_condita" class="mw-redirect" title="Ab Urbe condita">Ab Urbe condita</a></i>, meaning <i>"from the founding of the City"</i>, which counted the years from this presumed foundation.
</p>

<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Government">Government</h2></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_Rome" title="Mayor of Rome">Mayor of Rome</a>, <a href="/wiki/City_Council_of_Rome" title="City Council of Rome">City Council of Rome</a>, <a href="/wiki/Elections_in_Rome" title="Elections in Rome">Elections in Rome</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Administrative_subdivisions_of_Rome" title="Administrative subdivisions of Rome">Administrative subdivisions of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Musei_Capitolini_20150812.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Musei_Capitolini_20150812.jpg/250px-Musei_Capitolini_20150812.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Musei_Capitolini_20150812.jpg/500px-Musei_Capitolini_20150812.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5184" data-file-height="3456"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Piazza_del_Campidoglio" title="Piazza del Campidoglio">Palazzo Senatorio</a>, seat of the municipality of Rome. It has been a <a href="/wiki/Town_hall" title="Town hall">town hall</a> since 1144, making it the oldest town hall in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-Falconi_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Falconi-131"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Quirinale_palazzo_e_obelisco_con_dioscuri_Roma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Quirinale_palazzo_e_obelisco_con_dioscuri_Roma.jpg/250px-Quirinale_palazzo_e_obelisco_con_dioscuri_Roma.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="176" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Quirinale_palazzo_e_obelisco_con_dioscuri_Roma.jpg/500px-Quirinale_palazzo_e_obelisco_con_dioscuri_Roma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6965" data-file-height="4912"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Palazzo_del_Quirinale" class="mw-redirect" title="Palazzo del Quirinale">Palazzo del Quirinale</a>, current seat of the <a href="/wiki/President_of_Italy" title="President of Italy">President of the Italian Republic</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome constitutes a <i><a href="/wiki/Comune" title="Comune">comune</a> speciale</i>, named <i>"Roma Capitale"</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and is the largest both in terms of land area and population among the 8,101 <i>comuni</i> of Italy. It is governed by a mayor and a city council. The seat of the <i>comune</i> is the <i>Palazzo Senatorio</i> on the <a href="/wiki/Capitoline_Hill" title="Capitoline Hill">Capitoline Hill</a>, the historic seat of the city government. The local administration in Rome is commonly referred to as <i>"Campidoglio"</i>, the Italian name of the hill. <i>Palazzo Senatorio</i>, seat of the municipality of Rome, has been a <a href="/wiki/Town_hall" title="Town hall">town hall</a> since AD 1144, making it the oldest town hall in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-Falconi_131-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Falconi-131"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Since 1972, the city has been divided into administrative areas, called <i>municipi</i> (sing. <i>municipio</i>) (until 2001 named <i>circoscrizioni</i>).<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They were created for administrative reasons to increase decentralisation in the city. Each <i>municipio</i> is governed by a president and a council of twenty-five members who are elected by its residents every five years. The <i>municipi</i> frequently cross the boundaries of the traditional, non-administrative divisions of the city. The municipi were originally 20, then 19,<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and in 2013, their number was reduced to 15.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome is also divided into differing types of non-administrative units. The historic centre is divided into 22 <i><a href="/wiki/Rioni_of_Rome" title="Rioni of Rome">rioni</a></i>, all of which are located within the <a href="/wiki/Aurelian_Walls" title="Aurelian Walls">Aurelian Walls</a> except <a href="/wiki/Prati" title="Prati">Prati</a> and <a href="/wiki/Borgo_(rione_of_Rome)" title="Borgo (rione of Rome)">Borgo</a>. These originate from the <a href="/wiki/14_regions_of_Augustan_Rome" title="14 regions of Augustan Rome">14 regions of Augustan Rome</a>, which evolved in the Middle Ages into the <a href="/wiki/14_regions_of_Medieval_Rome" title="14 regions of Medieval Rome">medieval rioni</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>, under Pope <a href="/wiki/Sixtus_V" class="mw-redirect" title="Sixtus V">Sixtus V</a>, they again reached fourteen, and their boundaries were finally defined under <a href="/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XIV" title="Pope Benedict XIV">Pope Benedict XIV</a> in 1743.
</p><p>Rome is the principal town of the <a href="/wiki/Metropolitan_City_of_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Metropolitan City of Rome">Metropolitan City of Rome</a>, operative since 1 January 2015. The Metropolitan City replaced the old <a href="/wiki/Province_of_Rome" title="Province of Rome">provincia di Roma</a>, which included the city's metropolitan area and extends further north until <a href="/wiki/Civitavecchia" title="Civitavecchia">Civitavecchia</a>. The Metropolitan City of Rome is the largest by area in Italy. At 5,352 km<sup>2</sup> (2,066 sq mi), its dimensions are comparable to the region of <a href="/wiki/Liguria" title="Liguria">Liguria</a>. Moreover, the city is also the capital of the <a href="/wiki/Lazio" title="Lazio">Lazio</a> region.<sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome is the national capital of Italy and is the seat of the <a href="/wiki/Politics_of_Italy" title="Politics of Italy">Italian Government</a>. The official residences of the <a href="/wiki/President_of_Italy" title="President of Italy">President of the Italian Republic</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Italy" title="Prime Minister of Italy">Italian Prime Minister</a>, the seats of both houses of the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Italy" class="mw-redirect" title="Parliament of Italy">Italian Parliament</a> and that of the <a href="/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Italy" title="Constitutional Court of Italy">Italian Constitutional Court</a> are located in the historic centre. The state ministries are spread out around the city; these include the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is located in <a href="/wiki/Palazzo_della_Farnesina" title="Palazzo della Farnesina">Palazzo della Farnesina</a> near the Olympic stadium.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="International_relations">International relations</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_HQ_2008.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_HQ_2008.jpg/250px-Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_HQ_2008.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="149" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_HQ_2008.jpg/500px-Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_HQ_2008.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2025" data-file-height="1210"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization" title="Food and Agriculture Organization">Food and Agriculture Organization</a> headquarters in Rome, Circo Massimo</figcaption></figure>
<p>Among the <a href="/wiki/Global_cities" class="mw-redirect" title="Global cities">global cities</a>, Rome is unique in having two sovereign entities located entirely within its city limits, the Holy See, represented by the Vatican City State, and the territorially smaller <a href="/wiki/Sovereign_Military_Order_of_Malta" title="Sovereign Military Order of Malta">Sovereign Military Order of Malta</a>. The Vatican is an enclave of the Italian <a href="/wiki/Capital_city" title="Capital city">capital city</a> and a sovereign possession of the <a href="/wiki/Holy_See" title="Holy See">Holy See</a>, which is the Diocese of Rome and the supreme government of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholic Church">Roman Catholic Church</a>. For this reason, Rome has sometimes been described as the capital of two states.<sup id="cite_ref-138" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-138"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>135<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome is the seat of the so-called "Polo Romano" made up by three main international agencies of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>: the <a href="/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization" title="Food and Agriculture Organization">Food and Agriculture Organization</a>, the <a href="/wiki/World_Food_Programme" title="World Food Programme">World Food Programme</a> and the <a href="/wiki/International_Fund_for_Agricultural_Development" title="International Fund for Agricultural Development">International Fund for Agricultural Development</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome has traditionally been involved in the process of European political integration. The <a href="/wiki/Treaties_of_the_EU" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaties of the EU">Treaties of the EU</a> are located in <a href="/wiki/Palazzo_della_Farnesina" title="Palazzo della Farnesina">Palazzo della Farnesina</a>. In 1957 the city hosted the signing of the <a href="/wiki/Treaties_of_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaties of Rome">Treaty of Rome</a>, which established the <a href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</a> (predecessor to the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>), and also played host to the official signing of the proposed <a href="/wiki/Treaty_establishing_a_Constitution_for_Europe" title="Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe">European Constitution</a> in July 2004. Rome is the seat of the <a href="/wiki/European_Olympic_Committee" class="mw-redirect" title="European Olympic Committee">European Olympic Committee</a> and of the <a href="/wiki/NATO_Defense_College" title="NATO Defense College">NATO Defense College</a>. The city is the place where the <a href="/wiki/Rome_Statute_of_the_International_Criminal_Court" class="mw-redirect" title="Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court">Statute of the International Criminal Court</a> and the <a href="/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights" title="European Convention on Human Rights">European Convention on Human Rights</a> were formulated. The city hosts also other important international entities such as the <a href="/wiki/International_Development_Law_Organization" title="International Development Law Organization">International Development Law Organization</a>, the <a href="/wiki/International_Centre_for_the_Study_of_the_Preservation_and_Restoration_of_Cultural_Property" title="International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property">International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property</a> and the <a href="/wiki/UNIDROIT" title="UNIDROIT">UNIDROIT</a> (International Institute for the Unification of Private Law).
</p>

<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Economy">Economy</h2></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Economy_of_Rome" title="Economy of Rome">Economy of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Palazzo_Eni_(Rome)_in_2021.05.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Palazzo_Eni_%28Rome%29_in_2021.05.jpg/250px-Palazzo_Eni_%28Rome%29_in_2021.05.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Palazzo_Eni_%28Rome%29_in_2021.05.jpg/500px-Palazzo_Eni_%28Rome%29_in_2021.05.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4160" data-file-height="3120"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Palazzo_Eni" title="Palazzo Eni">Palazzo Eni</a>, in the <a href="/wiki/EUR,_Rome" title="EUR, Rome">EUR</a> <a href="/wiki/Business_district" class="mw-redirect" title="Business district">business district</a>, is the headquarters of <a href="/wiki/Eni" title="Eni">Eni</a>, considered one of the world's oil and gas "<a href="/wiki/Supermajors" class="mw-redirect" title="Supermajors">supermajors</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-162" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-162"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>158<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Roma_-_HQ_Enel_esterno.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Roma_-_HQ_Enel_esterno.jpg/250px-Roma_-_HQ_Enel_esterno.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Roma_-_HQ_Enel_esterno.jpg/500px-Roma_-_HQ_Enel_esterno.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4449" data-file-height="2966"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Enel" title="Enel">Enel</a>'s headquarters in Rome, the second largest <a href="/wiki/Power_company" class="mw-redirect" title="Power company">power company</a> in the world by revenue after the <a href="/wiki/State_Grid_Corporation_of_China" title="State Grid Corporation of China">State Grid Corporation of China</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-163" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-163"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>159<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Sede_BNL_Roma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Sede_BNL_Roma.jpg/250px-Sede_BNL_Roma.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="141" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Sede_BNL_Roma.jpg/500px-Sede_BNL_Roma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="1688"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Orizzonte_Europa" class="mw-redirect" title="Orizzonte Europa">Orizzonte Europa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Banca_Nazionale_del_Lavoro" title="Banca Nazionale del Lavoro">BNL</a> headquarters in Rome</figcaption></figure>
<p>As the capital of Italy, Rome hosts all the principal institutions of the nation, including the Presidency of the Republic, the government (and its single <span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it">Ministeri</i></span>), the Parliament, the main judicial Courts, and the diplomatic representatives of all the countries for the states of Italy and Vatican City. Many international institutions are located in Rome, notably cultural and scientific ones, such as the American Institute, the British School, the French Academy, the Scandinavian Institutes, and the German Archaeological Institute. There are also specialized agencies of the United Nations, such as the <a href="/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization" title="Food and Agriculture Organization">Food and Agriculture Organization</a>. Rome also hosts major international and worldwide political and cultural organizations, such as the <a href="/wiki/International_Fund_for_Agricultural_Development" title="International Fund for Agricultural Development">International Fund for Agricultural Development</a>, <a href="/wiki/World_Food_Programme" title="World Food Programme">World Food Programme</a>, the <a href="/wiki/NATO_Defence_College" class="mw-redirect" title="NATO Defence College">NATO Defence College</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/International_Centre_for_the_Study_of_the_Preservation_and_Restoration_of_Cultural_Property" title="International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property">International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property</a>.
</p><p>According to the <a href="/wiki/Global_city#GaWC_study" title="Global city">GaWC study of world cities</a>, Rome is a "Beta +" city.<sup id="cite_ref-GAWC_164-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GAWC-164"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>160<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The city was ranked in 2024 as 31st in the Global Cities Index, second highest in Italy after Milan.<sup id="cite_ref-atkearney.at_165-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-atkearney.at-165"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>161<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> With a 2005 GDP of €94.376 billion (US$121.5 billion),<sup id="cite_ref-rapporto2006_166-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rapporto2006-166"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="This information is in need of an update. (May 2018)">needs update</span></a></i>]</sup> the city produces 6.7% of the national GDP (more than any other single city in Italy), and its unemployment rate, lowered from 11.1% to 6.5% between 2001 and 2005, is now one of the lowest rates of all the European Union capital cities.<sup id="cite_ref-rapporto2006_166-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rapporto2006-166"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome's economy grows at around 4.4% annually and continues to grow at a higher rate in comparison to any other city in the rest of the country.<sup id="cite_ref-rapporto2006_166-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rapporto2006-166"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This means that were Rome a country, it would be the world's 52nd richest country by GDP, near to the size to that of Egypt. Rome also had a 2003 GDP per capita of €29,153 (US$37,412), which was second in Italy (after Milan), and is more than 134.1% of the EU average GDP per capita.<sup id="cite_ref-observatoribarcelona.org_167-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-observatoribarcelona.org-167"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>163<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="This information is in need of an update. (May 2018)">needs update</span></a></i>]</sup> Rome, on the whole, has the highest total earnings in Italy, reaching €47,076,890,463 in 2008,<sup id="cite_ref-ilsole24ore.com_168-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ilsole24ore.com-168"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="This information is in need of an update. (May 2018)">needs update</span></a></i>]</sup> yet, in terms of average workers' incomes, the city places itself 9th in Italy, with €24,509.<sup id="cite_ref-ilsole24ore.com_168-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ilsole24ore.com-168"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On a global level, Rome's workers received the 30th highest wages in 2009, coming three places higher than in 2008, in which the city ranked 33rd.<sup id="cite_ref-citymayors_a_169-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-citymayors_a-169"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>165<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="This information is in need of an update. (May 2018)">needs update</span></a></i>]</sup> In 2023, the Rome area had a <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_by_GDP" title="List of cities by GDP">GDP amounting to $240.73 billion</a>, and $57,142 per capita.<sup id="cite_ref-Brookings_170-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brookings-170"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>166<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Although the economy of Rome is characterized by the absence of heavy industry, and it is largely dominated by <a href="/wiki/Service_(economics)" title="Service (economics)">services</a>, high-technology companies (IT, aerospace, defense, telecommunications, accelerators, incubators, start-ups ), research, construction and commercial activities (especially banking and insurance), and the huge development of tourism are very dynamic and extremely important to its economy. With over 50 million passengers in 2025, Rome's <a href="/wiki/Rome_Fiumicino_Airport" title="Rome Fiumicino Airport">Leonardo Da Vinci Intercontinental Airport</a>, also known as <a href="/wiki/Fiumicino" title="Fiumicino">Fiumicino</a>, is the largest and busiest in Italy as well as one of the giant European hubs.
</p><p>In addition the city hosts the head offices of the vast majority of the biggest Italian companies, as well as the headquarters of three of the world's 100 largest companies: <a href="/wiki/Enel" title="Enel">Enel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Eni" title="Eni">Eni</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Telecom_Italia" class="mw-redirect" title="Telecom Italia">Telecom Italia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Forbes_171-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forbes-171"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>167<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Universities, national radio and television and the movie industry in Rome are also important parts of the economy: Rome is also the hub of the <a href="/wiki/Cinema_of_Italy" title="Cinema of Italy">Italian film industry</a>, thanks to the Cinecittà Studios, working since the 1930s. The city is also a centre for banking and insurance as well as electronics, energy, transport, and aerospace industries. Numerous international companies and agencies headquarters, government ministries, conference centres, sports venues, and museums are located in Rome's principal business districts: the <a href="/wiki/Esposizione_Universale_Roma" class="mw-redirect" title="Esposizione Universale Roma">Esposizione Universale Roma</a> (EUR); the <i>Torrino</i> (further south from the EUR); the <i>Magliana</i>; the <i>Parco de' Medici-Laurentina</i> and the so-called <i>Tiburtina-valley</i> along the ancient <a href="/wiki/Via_Tiburtina" title="Via Tiburtina">Via Tiburtina</a>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Tourism">Tourism</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Tourism_in_Rome" title="Tourism in Rome">Tourism in Rome</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_tourist_attractions_in_Rome" title="List of tourist attractions in Rome">List of tourist attractions in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Spanish_Steps,_Rome_(47509253002).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/The_Spanish_Steps%2C_Rome_%2847509253002%29.jpg/250px-The_Spanish_Steps%2C_Rome_%2847509253002%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/The_Spanish_Steps%2C_Rome_%2847509253002%29.jpg/500px-The_Spanish_Steps%2C_Rome_%2847509253002%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6004" data-file-height="3954"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Fontana_della_Barcaccia" title="Fontana della Barcaccia">Fontana della Barcaccia</a> in <a href="/wiki/Piazza_di_Spagna" title="Piazza di Spagna">Piazza di Spagna</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Spanish_Steps" title="Spanish Steps">Spanish Steps</a> and <a href="/wiki/Trinit%C3%A0_dei_Monti" title="Trinità dei Monti">Trinità dei Monti</a></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Empty_Piazza_Navona_(85148359).jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Empty_Piazza_Navona_%2885148359%29.jpeg/250px-Empty_Piazza_Navona_%2885148359%29.jpeg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Empty_Piazza_Navona_%2885148359%29.jpeg/500px-Empty_Piazza_Navona_%2885148359%29.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1357"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Piazza_Navona" title="Piazza Navona">Piazza Navona</a></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Vatican_Museums_Spiral_Staircase_2012.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Vatican_Museums_Spiral_Staircase_2012.jpg/250px-Vatican_Museums_Spiral_Staircase_2012.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="159" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Vatican_Museums_Spiral_Staircase_2012.jpg/500px-Vatican_Museums_Spiral_Staircase_2012.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4336" data-file-height="2756"></a><figcaption>As of 2022<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rome&action=edit">[update]</a></sup>, the <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Museums" title="Vatican Museums">Vatican Museums</a> are the <a href="/wiki/List_of_most_visited_art_museums" class="mw-redirect" title="List of most visited art museums">second most visited art museum</a> in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-172"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>168<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome today is one of the most important tourist destinations of the world, due to the incalculable immensity of its archaeological and artistic treasures, as well as for the charm of its unique traditions, the beauty of its panoramic views, and the majesty of its magnificent "villas" (parks). Among the most significant resources are the many museums – <a href="/wiki/Capitoline_Museums" title="Capitoline Museums">Capitoline Museums</a>, <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Museums" title="Vatican Museums">the Vatican Museums</a> and the <span title="Italian-language text"><span lang="it" style="font-style: normal;"><a href="/wiki/Galleria_Borghese" title="Galleria Borghese">Galleria Borghese</a></span></span> and others dedicated to modern and contemporary art – <a href="/wiki/Aqueduct_(watercourse)" class="mw-redirect" title="Aqueduct (watercourse)">aqueducts</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fountain" title="Fountain">fountains</a>, churches, <a href="/wiki/Palace" title="Palace">palaces</a>, historical buildings, the <a href="/wiki/Monument" title="Monument">monuments</a> and ruins of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Forum" title="Roman Forum">Roman Forum</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Catacombs" title="Catacombs">Catacombs</a>. Rome is the third most visited city in the EU, after London and Paris, and receives an average of 7–10 million tourists a year, which sometimes doubles on holy years. The Colosseum (4 million tourists) and the <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Museums" title="Vatican Museums">Vatican Museums</a> (4.2 million tourists) are the 39th and 37th (respectively) most visited places in the world, according to a recent study.<sup id="cite_ref-itvnews.tv_173-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-itvnews.tv-173"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>169<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome is a major archaeological hub, and one of the world's main centres of <a href="/wiki/Archaeology" title="Archaeology">archaeological research</a>. There are numerous cultural and research institutes located in the city, such as the <a href="/wiki/American_Academy_in_Rome" title="American Academy in Rome">American Academy in Rome</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and The Swedish Institute at Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>171<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome contains numerous <a href="/wiki/List_of_ancient_monuments_in_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="List of ancient monuments in Rome">ancient sites</a>, including the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Forum" title="Roman Forum">Forum Romanum</a>, <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Market" title="Trajan's Market">Trajan's Market</a>, <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Forum" title="Trajan's Forum">Trajan's Forum</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>172<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Colosseum" title="Colosseum">Colosseum</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome" title="Pantheon, Rome">Pantheon</a>, to name but a few. The <a href="/wiki/Colosseum" title="Colosseum">Colosseum</a>, arguably one of Rome's most iconic archaeological sites, is regarded as a <a href="/wiki/Wonders_of_the_World" title="Wonders of the World">wonder of the world</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-brewers_177-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-brewers-177"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>173<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-miller_178-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-miller-178"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>174<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome contains a vast collection of art, sculpture, <a href="/wiki/Fountain" title="Fountain">fountains</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mosaic" title="Mosaic">mosaics</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fresco" title="Fresco">frescos</a>, and paintings, from all different periods. Rome first became a major artistic centre during ancient Rome, with forms of important <a href="/wiki/Roman_art" title="Roman art">Roman art</a> such as <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_ancient_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Architecture of ancient Rome">architecture</a>, painting, sculpture and <a href="/wiki/Mosaic" title="Mosaic">mosaic</a> work. <a href="/wiki/Metalworking" title="Metalworking">Metal-work</a>, <a href="/wiki/Coin_die" class="mw-redirect" title="Coin die">coin die</a> and gem engraving, <a href="/wiki/Ivory_carving" title="Ivory carving">ivory carvings</a>, figurine glass, <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Roman_pottery" title="Ancient Roman pottery">pottery</a>, and book illustrations are considered to be 'minor' forms of Roman artwork.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>175<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome later became a major centre of <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a> art, since the popes spent vast sums of money for the constructions of grandiose <a href="/wiki/Basilica" title="Basilica">basilicas</a>, <a href="/wiki/Palace" title="Palace">palaces</a>, <a href="/wiki/Piazza" class="mw-redirect" title="Piazza">piazzas</a> and public buildings in general. Rome became one of Europe's major centres of Renaissance artwork along with <a href="/wiki/Florence" title="Florence">Florence</a>, and able to compare to other major cities and cultural centres, such as Paris and <a href="/wiki/Venice" title="Venice">Venice</a>. Some of the greatest artists of this time found work in Rome: <a href="/wiki/Michelangelo" title="Michelangelo">Michelangelo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Raffaello_Sanzio" class="mw-redirect" title="Raffaello Sanzio">Raffaello Sanzio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Donato_Bramante" title="Donato Bramante">Donato Bramante</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sandro_Botticelli" title="Sandro Botticelli">Sandro Botticelli</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ghirlandaio" title="Ghirlandaio">Ghirlandaio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Piero_della_Francesca" title="Piero della Francesca">Piero della Francesca</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pietro_Perugino" title="Pietro Perugino">Pietro Perugino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cosimo_Rosselli" title="Cosimo Rosselli">Cosimo Rosselli</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gentile_da_Fabriano" title="Gentile da Fabriano">Gentile da Fabriano</a>, <a href="/wiki/Beato_Angelico" class="mw-redirect" title="Beato Angelico">Beato Angelico</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leon_Battista_Alberti" title="Leon Battista Alberti">Leon Battista Alberti</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Giovanni_Battista_Penni&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Giovanni Battista Penni (page does not exist)">Giovanni Battista Penni</a>, <a href="/wiki/Giulio_Romano" title="Giulio Romano">Giulio Romano</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rosso_Fiorentino" title="Rosso Fiorentino">Rosso Fiorentino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Parmigianino" title="Parmigianino">Parmigianino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bernardo_Rossellino" title="Bernardo Rossellino">Bernardo Rossellino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Benozzo_Gozzoli" title="Benozzo Gozzoli">Benozzo Gozzoli</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pisanello" title="Pisanello">Pisanello</a> and others. The city was affected greatly by the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Baroque" title="Italian Baroque">baroque</a>, and Rome became the home of numerous artists and architects, such as <a href="/wiki/Gian_Lorenzo_Bernini" title="Gian Lorenzo Bernini">Bernini</a>, <a href="/wiki/Caravaggio" title="Caravaggio">Caravaggio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Annibale_Carracci" title="Annibale Carracci">Carracci</a>, <a href="/wiki/Francesco_Borromini" title="Francesco Borromini">Borromini</a>, <a href="/wiki/Stefano_Maderno" title="Stefano Maderno">Stefano Maderno</a>, <a href="/wiki/Francesco_Mochi" title="Francesco Mochi">Francesco Mochi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Domenichino" title="Domenichino">Domenichino</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Pietro_Paolo_Rubens&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Pietro Paolo Rubens (page does not exist)">Pietro Paolo Rubens</a>, <a href="/wiki/Guido_Reni" title="Guido Reni">Guido Reni</a>, <a href="/wiki/Diego_Vel%C3%A1zquez" title="Diego Velázquez">Diego Velázquez</a>, <a href="/wiki/Artemisia_Gentileschi" title="Artemisia Gentileschi">Artemisia Gentileschi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Orazio_Gentileschi" title="Orazio Gentileschi">Orazio Gentileschi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Andrea_Pozzo" title="Andrea Pozzo">Andrea Pozzo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Baciccia" class="mw-redirect" title="Baciccia">Baciccia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pietro_da_Cortona" title="Pietro da Cortona">Cortona</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>176<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In the late 18th century and early 19th century, the city was one of the centres of the <a href="/wiki/Grand_Tour" class="mw-redirect" title="Grand Tour">Grand Tour</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>177<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> when wealthy, young English and other European aristocrats visited the city to learn about <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_ancient_Rome" title="Culture of ancient Rome">ancient Roman culture</a>, art, philosophy, and architecture. Rome hosted a great number of neoclassical and rococo artists, such as <a href="/wiki/Giovanni_Paolo_Pannini" class="mw-redirect" title="Giovanni Paolo Pannini">Pannini</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bernardo_Bellotto" title="Bernardo Bellotto">Bernardo Bellotto</a>. Today, the city is a major artistic centre, with numerous art institutes<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>178<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and museums.
</p><p>Rome has a growing stock of contemporary and modern art and architecture. The National Gallery of Modern Art has works by Balla, Morandi, Pirandello, Carrà, De Chirico, De Pisis, Guttuso, Fontana, Burri, Mastroianni, Turcato, Kandisky, and Cézanne on permanent exhibition. 2010 saw the opening of Rome's newest arts foundation, a contemporary art and architecture gallery designed by acclaimed Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. Known as <a href="/wiki/MAXXI_%E2%80%93_National_Museum_of_the_21st_Century_Arts" class="mw-redirect" title="MAXXI – National Museum of the 21st Century Arts">MAXXI – National Museum of the 21st Century Arts</a> it restores a dilapidated area with striking modern architecture. Maxxi<sup id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-183"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>179<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> features a campus dedicated to culture, experimental research laboratories, international exchange and study and research. It is one of Rome's most ambitious modern architecture projects alongside <a href="/wiki/Renzo_Piano" title="Renzo Piano">Renzo Piano</a>'s Auditorium Parco della Musica<sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>180<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Massimiliano_Fuksas" title="Massimiliano Fuksas">Massimiliano Fuksas</a>' Rome Convention Center, Centro Congressi Italia EUR, in the EUR district, due to open in 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>181<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The convention centre features a huge translucent container inside which is suspended a steel and teflon structure resembling a cloud and which contains meeting rooms and an auditorium with two piazzas open to the neighbourhood on either side.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Education">Education</h2></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Sede_Sapienza.jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Sede_Sapienza.jpeg/250px-Sede_Sapienza.jpeg" decoding="async" width="250" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Sede_Sapienza.jpeg/500px-Sede_Sapienza.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="2926" data-file-height="1709"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Sapienza_University_of_Rome" title="Sapienza University of Rome">Sapienza University of Rome</a>. It was founded in 1303 and is as such one of the world's oldest universities,<sup id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-186"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>182<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and with 122,000 students, it is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_largest_universities_by_enrollment" class="mw-redirect" title="List of largest universities by enrollment">largest university in Europe</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-187"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>183<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is a nationwide and major international centre for higher education, containing numerous academies, colleges and universities. It boasts a large variety of academies and colleges, and has always been a major worldwide intellectual and educational centre, especially during <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Ancient Rome</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>, along with Florence.<sup id="cite_ref-188" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-188"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>184<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to the City Brands Index, Rome is considered the world's second most historically, educationally and culturally interesting and beautiful city.<sup id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-189"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>185<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Rome has many universities and colleges. Its first university, <a href="/wiki/Sapienza_University_of_Rome" title="Sapienza University of Rome">La Sapienza</a> (founded in 1303), is one of the largest in the world, with more than 140,000 students attending; in 2005 it ranked as Europe's 33rd best university<sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>186<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and in 2013 the Sapienza University of Rome ranked as the 62nd in the world and the top in Italy in its <i>World University Rankings</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-191"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>187<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and has been ranked among Europe's 50 and the world's 150 best colleges.<sup id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-192"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>188<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In order to decrease the overcrowding of La Sapienza, two new public universities were founded during the last decades: <a href="/wiki/University_of_Rome_Tor_Vergata" title="University of Rome Tor Vergata">Tor Vergata</a> in 1982, and <a href="/wiki/Roma_Tre_University" title="Roma Tre University">Roma Tre</a> in 1992. Rome hosts also the <a href="/wiki/LUISS_School_of_Government" title="LUISS School of Government">LUISS School of Government</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-193"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>189<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Italy's most important graduate university in the areas of international affairs and European studies as well as <a href="/wiki/LUISS_Business_School" title="LUISS Business School">LUISS Business School</a>, Italy's most important business school. Rome <a href="/wiki/Istituto_superiore_per_le_industrie_artistiche_(ISIA)" class="mw-redirect" title="Istituto superiore per le industrie artistiche (ISIA)">ISIA</a> was founded in 1973 by <a href="/wiki/Giulio_Carlo_Argan" title="Giulio Carlo Argan">Giulio Carlo Argan</a> and is Italy's oldest institution in the field of <a href="/wiki/Industrial_design" title="Industrial design">industrial design</a>.
</p>
