<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Biblioteca_Casanatense.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Biblioteca_Casanatense.jpg/250px-Biblioteca_Casanatense.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Biblioteca_Casanatense.jpg/500px-Biblioteca_Casanatense.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1649" data-file-height="1081"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Biblioteca_Casanatense" title="Biblioteca Casanatense">Biblioteca Casanatense</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome contains many <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_university" class="mw-redirect" title="Pontifical university">pontifical universities</a> and other institutes, including the <a href="/wiki/British_School_at_Rome" title="British School at Rome">British School at Rome</a>, the <a href="/wiki/French_Academy_in_Rome" title="French Academy in Rome">French School in Rome</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Gregorian_University" title="Pontifical Gregorian University">Pontifical Gregorian University</a> (the oldest <a href="/wiki/Society_of_Jesus" class="mw-redirect" title="Society of Jesus">Jesuit</a> university in the world, founded in 1551), <a href="/wiki/Istituto_Europeo_di_Design" title="Istituto Europeo di Design">Istituto Europeo di Design</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Lorenzo_de%27_Medici_School" title="Lorenzo de' Medici School">Scuola Lorenzo de' Medici</a>, the Link <a href="/wiki/Link_Campus" class="mw-redirect" title="Link Campus">Campus of Malta</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Universit%C3%A0_Campus_Bio-Medico" class="mw-redirect" title="Università Campus Bio-Medico">Università Campus Bio-Medico</a>. Rome is also the location of two American Universities; <a href="/wiki/The_American_University_of_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="The American University of Rome">The American University of Rome</a><sup id="cite_ref-194" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-194"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>190<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/John_Cabot_University" title="John Cabot University">John Cabot University</a> as well as <a href="/wiki/St._John%27s_University_(Italy)" title="St. John's University (Italy)">St. John's University</a> branch campus, <a href="/wiki/John_Felice_Rome_Center" title="John Felice Rome Center">John Felice Rome Center</a>, a campus of <a href="/wiki/Loyola_University_Chicago" title="Loyola University Chicago">Loyola University Chicago</a> and Temple University Rome, a campus of <a href="/wiki/Temple_University" title="Temple University">Temple University</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-195" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-195"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>191<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Roman_Colleges" title="Roman Colleges">Roman Colleges</a> are several <a href="/wiki/Seminary" title="Seminary">seminaries</a> for students from foreign countries studying for the <a href="/wiki/Catholic_priesthood" class="mw-redirect" title="Catholic priesthood">priesthood</a> at the Pontifical Universities.<sup id="cite_ref-NAC_196-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NAC-196"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>192<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Examples include the <a href="/wiki/Venerable_English_College" class="mw-redirect" title="Venerable English College">Venerable English College</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_North_American_College" title="Pontifical North American College">Pontifical North American College</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Scots_College_(Rome)" title="Scots College (Rome)">Scots College</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Pontifical_Croatian_College_of_St._Jerome" title="Pontifical Croatian College of St. Jerome">Pontifical Croatian College of St. Jerome</a>. Rome's major libraries include: the <span title="Italian-language text"><span lang="it" style="font-style: normal;"><a href="/wiki/Biblioteca_Angelica" title="Biblioteca Angelica">Biblioteca Angelica</a></span></span>, opened in 1604, making it Italy's first public library; the <a href="/wiki/Biblioteca_Vallicelliana" title="Biblioteca Vallicelliana">Biblioteca Vallicelliana</a>, established in 1565; the <a href="/wiki/Biblioteca_Casanatense" title="Biblioteca Casanatense">Biblioteca Casanatense</a>, opened in 1701; the <a href="/wiki/National_Central_Library_(Rome)" class="mw-redirect" title="National Central Library (Rome)">National Central Library</a>, one of the two national libraries in Italy, which contains 4,126,002 volumes; The Biblioteca del Ministero degli Affari Esteri, specialised in diplomacy, foreign affairs and modern history; the Biblioteca dell'Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana; the Biblioteca Don Bosco, one of the largest and most modern of all Salesian libraries; the Biblioteca e Museo teatrale del Burcardo, a museum-library specialised in history of drama and theatre; the Biblioteca della <a href="/wiki/Societ%C3%A0_Geografica_Italiana" title="Società Geografica Italiana">Società Geografica Italiana</a>, which is based in the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Mattei" class="mw-redirect" title="Villa Mattei">Villa Celimontana</a> and is the most important geographical library in Italy, and one of Europe's most important;<sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>193<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Library" title="Vatican Library">Vatican Library</a>, one of the oldest and most important libraries in the world, which was formally established in 1475, though in fact much older and has 75,000 <a href="/wiki/Codex" title="Codex">codices</a>, as well as 1.1 million printed books, which include some 8,500 <a href="/wiki/Incunabulum" class="mw-redirect" title="Incunabulum">incunabula</a>. There are also many specialist libraries attached to various foreign cultural institutes in Rome, among them that of the <a href="/wiki/American_Academy_in_Rome" title="American Academy in Rome">American Academy in Rome</a>, the <a href="/wiki/French_Academy_in_Rome" title="French Academy in Rome">French Academy in Rome</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Bibliotheca_Hertziana_%E2%80%93_Max_Planck_Institute_of_Art_History" class="mw-redirect" title="Bibliotheca Hertziana – Max Planck Institute of Art History">Bibliotheca Hertziana – Max Planck Institute of Art History</a>, a German library, often noted for excellence in the arts and sciences.<sup id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-198"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>194<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Culture">Culture</h2></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Culture_in_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Culture in Rome">Culture in Rome</a></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Architecture">Architecture</h3></div>
<div class="excerpt-block"><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1066933788">.mw-parser-output .excerpt-hat .mw-editsection-like{font-style:normal}</style><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable dablink excerpt-hat selfref">This section is an excerpt from <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Rome" title="Architecture of Rome">Architecture of Rome</a>.<span class="mw-editsection-like plainlinks"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Architecture_of_Rome&action=edit">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div><div class="excerpt">
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Rome" title="Architecture of Rome">architecture of Rome</a> over the centuries has greatly developed from <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Roman_architecture" title="Ancient Roman architecture">Ancient Roman architecture</a> to <a href="/wiki/Italian_modern_and_contemporary_architecture" title="Italian modern and contemporary architecture">Italian modern and contemporary architecture</a>. Rome was once the world's main epicentres of <a href="/wiki/Classical_architecture" title="Classical architecture">Classical architecture</a>, developing new forms such as the <a href="/wiki/Arch" title="Arch">arch</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Dome" title="Dome">dome</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Vault_(architecture)" title="Vault (architecture)">vault</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Romanesque_architecture" title="Romanesque architecture">Romanesque</a> style in the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries was also widely used in Roman <a href="/wiki/Architecture" title="Architecture">architecture</a>, and later the city became one of the main centres of <a href="/wiki/Renaissance_architecture" title="Renaissance architecture">Renaissance</a> and <a href="/wiki/Baroque_architecture" title="Baroque architecture">Baroque architecture</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Architecture_of_Rome_r1_199-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Architecture_of_Rome_r1-199"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>195<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rome's cityscape is also widely <a href="/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture" title="Neoclassical architecture">Neoclassical</a> and <a href="/wiki/Fascist_architecture" title="Fascist architecture">Fascist</a> in style.
</p>
</div></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Palazzo_della_civilt%C3%A0_del_lavoro_(EUR,_Rome)_(5904657870).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Palazzo_della_civilt%C3%A0_del_lavoro_%28EUR%2C_Rome%29_%285904657870%29.jpg/250px-Palazzo_della_civilt%C3%A0_del_lavoro_%28EUR%2C_Rome%29_%285904657870%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Palazzo_della_civilt%C3%A0_del_lavoro_%28EUR%2C_Rome%29_%285904657870%29.jpg/500px-Palazzo_della_civilt%C3%A0_del_lavoro_%28EUR%2C_Rome%29_%285904657870%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1800" data-file-height="1200"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Palazzo_della_Civilt%C3%A0_Italiana" title="Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana">Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana</a> in <a href="/wiki/EUR,_Rome" title="EUR, Rome">EUR district</a></figcaption></figure>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Fountains_and_aqueducts">Fountains and aqueducts</h4></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/List_of_fountains_in_Rome" title="List of fountains in Rome">List of fountains in Rome</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_aqueducts_in_the_city_of_Rome" title="List of aqueducts in the city of Rome">List of aqueducts in the city of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Trevi_Fountain,_Rome,_Italy_2_-_May_2007.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Trevi_Fountain%2C_Rome%2C_Italy_2_-_May_2007.jpg/250px-Trevi_Fountain%2C_Rome%2C_Italy_2_-_May_2007.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Trevi_Fountain%2C_Rome%2C_Italy_2_-_May_2007.jpg/500px-Trevi_Fountain%2C_Rome%2C_Italy_2_-_May_2007.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3500" data-file-height="2325"></a><figcaption>Construction of the <a href="/wiki/Trevi_Fountain" title="Trevi Fountain">Trevi Fountain</a> began during the time of Ancient Rome and was completed in 1762 by a design of <a href="/wiki/Nicola_Salvi" title="Nicola Salvi">Nicola Salvi</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is a city known for its numerous fountains, built-in all different styles, from Classical and Medieval, to Baroque and Neoclassical. The city has had <a href="/wiki/Fountain" title="Fountain">fountains</a> for more than two thousand years, and they have provided drinking water and decorated the <a href="/wiki/Piazza" class="mw-redirect" title="Piazza">piazzas</a> of Rome. During the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</a>, in 98 AD, according to <a href="/wiki/Sextus_Julius_Frontinus" class="mw-redirect" title="Sextus Julius Frontinus">Sextus Julius Frontinus</a>, the Roman consul who was named <i><a href="/wiki/Curator_Aquarum" title="Curator Aquarum">curator aquarum</a></i> or guardian of the water of the city, Rome had nine <a href="/wiki/Aqueduct_(watercourse)" class="mw-redirect" title="Aqueduct (watercourse)">aqueducts</a> which fed 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins, not counting the water supplied to the Imperial household, baths, and owners of private villas. Each of the major fountains was connected to two different aqueducts, in case one was shut down for service.<sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>196<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During the 17th and 18th century, the Roman popes reconstructed other degraded Roman aqueducts and built new display fountains to mark their termini, launching the golden age of the Roman fountain. The fountains of Rome, like the paintings of <a href="/wiki/Peter_Paul_Rubens" title="Peter Paul Rubens">Rubens</a>, were expressions of the new style of Baroque art. In these fountains, sculpture became the principal element, and the water was used simply to animate and decorate the sculptures. They, like baroque gardens, were "a visual representation of confidence and power".<sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>197<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Statues">Statues</h4></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Talking_statues_of_Rome" title="Talking statues of Rome">Talking statues of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Vierstr%C3%B6mebrunnen-Fontana_dei_Quattro_Fiumi_(27903447766).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Vierstr%C3%B6mebrunnen-Fontana_dei_Quattro_Fiumi_%2827903447766%29.jpg/250px-Vierstr%C3%B6mebrunnen-Fontana_dei_Quattro_Fiumi_%2827903447766%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Vierstr%C3%B6mebrunnen-Fontana_dei_Quattro_Fiumi_%2827903447766%29.jpg/500px-Vierstr%C3%B6mebrunnen-Fontana_dei_Quattro_Fiumi_%2827903447766%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2496" data-file-height="1664"></a><figcaption>Fontana dei Fiumi by <a href="/wiki/Gian_Lorenzo_Bernini" title="Gian Lorenzo Bernini">Gian Lorenzo Bernini</a>, 1648</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is well known for its statues but, in particular, the <a href="/wiki/Talking_statues_of_Rome" title="Talking statues of Rome">talking statues of Rome</a>. These are usually ancient statues which have become popular soapboxes for political and social discussion, and places for people to (often satirically) voice their opinions. There are two main talking statues: the <a href="/wiki/Pasquino" title="Pasquino">Pasquino</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Marforio" title="Marforio">Marforio</a>, yet there are four other noted ones: <i><a href="/wiki/Il_Babuino" class="mw-redirect" title="Il Babuino">il Babuino</a></i>, <a href="/wiki/Madama_Lucrezia" title="Madama Lucrezia">Madama Lucrezia</a>, <i><a href="/wiki/Il_Facchino" title="Il Facchino">il Facchino</a></i> and <a href="/wiki/Abbot_Luigi" title="Abbot Luigi">Abbot Luigi</a>. Most of these statues are ancient Roman or classical, and most of them also depict mythical gods, ancient people or legendary figures; il Pasquino represents <a href="/wiki/Menelaus" title="Menelaus">Menelaus</a>, Abbot Luigi is an unknown Roman magistrate, <i>il Babuino</i> is supposed to be <a href="/wiki/Silenus" title="Silenus">Silenus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Marforio" title="Marforio">Marforio</a> represents <a href="/wiki/Oceanus" title="Oceanus">Oceanus</a>, Madama Lucrezia is a bust of <a href="/wiki/Isis" title="Isis">Isis</a>, and <i><a href="/wiki/Il_Facchino" title="Il Facchino">il Facchino</a></i> is the only non-Roman statue, created in 1580, and not representing anyone in particular. They are often, due to their status, covered with placards or <a href="/wiki/Graffiti" title="Graffiti">graffiti</a> expressing political ideas and points of view. Other statues in the city, which are not related to the talking statues, include those of the Ponte Sant'Angelo, or several monuments scattered across the city, such as that to <a href="/wiki/Giordano_Bruno" title="Giordano Bruno">Giordano Bruno</a> in the Campo de'Fiori.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Obelisks_and_columns">Obelisks and columns</h4></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_obelisks_in_Rome" title="List of obelisks in Rome">List of obelisks in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Piazza_del_Popolo_Obelisco_Flaminio_a_Roma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Piazza_del_Popolo_Obelisco_Flaminio_a_Roma.jpg/250px-Piazza_del_Popolo_Obelisco_Flaminio_a_Roma.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Piazza_del_Popolo_Obelisco_Flaminio_a_Roma.jpg/500px-Piazza_del_Popolo_Obelisco_Flaminio_a_Roma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="7360" data-file-height="4912"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Flaminio_Obelisk" title="Flaminio Obelisk">Flaminio Obelisk</a>, <a href="/wiki/Piazza_del_Popolo" title="Piazza del Popolo">Piazza del Popolo</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The city hosts eight <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Egypt" title="Ancient Egypt">ancient Egyptian</a> and five <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">ancient Roman</a> <a href="/wiki/Obelisk" title="Obelisk">obelisks</a>, together with a number of more modern obelisks; there was also formerly (until 2005) an <a href="/wiki/Aksumite_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Aksumite Empire">ancient Ethiopian</a> obelisk in Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-202"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>198<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The city contains some of obelisks in <a href="/wiki/Piazza" class="mw-redirect" title="Piazza">piazzas</a>, such as in <a href="/wiki/Piazza_Navona" title="Piazza Navona">Piazza Navona</a>, <a href="/wiki/Saint_Peter%27s_Square" class="mw-redirect" title="Saint Peter's Square">St Peter's Square</a>, <a href="/wiki/Piazza_di_Monte_Citorio" title="Piazza di Monte Citorio">Piazza Montecitorio</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Piazza_del_Popolo" title="Piazza del Popolo">Piazza del Popolo</a>, and others in <a href="/wiki/Villa" title="Villa">villas</a>, <a href="/wiki/Thermae" title="Thermae">thermae</a> parks and gardens, such as in <a href="/wiki/Villa_Mattei" class="mw-redirect" title="Villa Mattei">Villa Celimontana</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Baths_of_Diocletian" title="Baths of Diocletian">Baths of Diocletian</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Pincian_Hill" title="Pincian Hill">Pincian Hill</a>. Moreover, the centre of Rome hosts also <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Column" title="Trajan's Column">Trajan</a>'s and <a href="/wiki/Column_of_Marcus_Aurelius" title="Column of Marcus Aurelius">Antonine Column</a>, two ancient Roman columns with spiral relief. The Column of Marcus Aurelius is located in <a href="/wiki/Piazza_Colonna" title="Piazza Colonna">Piazza Colonna</a> and it was built around AD 180 by <a href="/wiki/Commodus" title="Commodus">Commodus</a> in memory of his parents. The <a href="/wiki/Column_of_Marcus_Aurelius" title="Column of Marcus Aurelius">Column of Marcus Aurelius</a> was inspired by <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Column" title="Trajan's Column">Trajan's Column</a> at <a href="/wiki/Trajan%27s_Forum" title="Trajan's Forum">Trajan's Forum</a>, which is part of the <a href="/wiki/Imperial_Fora" class="mw-redirect" title="Imperial Fora">Imperial Fora</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-203"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>199<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Bridges">Bridges</h4></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_bridges_in_Rome" title="List of bridges in Rome">List of bridges in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Bridge_Vittorio_Emanuele_II_at_sunset.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Bridge_Vittorio_Emanuele_II_at_sunset.jpg/250px-Bridge_Vittorio_Emanuele_II_at_sunset.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Bridge_Vittorio_Emanuele_II_at_sunset.jpg/500px-Bridge_Vittorio_Emanuele_II_at_sunset.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5716" data-file-height="3848"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ponte_Vittorio_Emanuele_II" title="Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II">Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II</a> at sunset</figcaption></figure>
<p>The city of Rome contains numerous famous bridges which cross the <a href="/wiki/Tiber" title="Tiber">Tiber</a>. The only bridge to remain unaltered until today from the classical age is <a href="/wiki/Pons_Fabricius" title="Pons Fabricius">Ponte dei Quattro Capi</a>, which connects the <a href="/wiki/Isola_Tiberina" class="mw-redirect" title="Isola Tiberina">Isola Tiberina</a> with the left bank. The other surviving – albeit modified – ancient Roman bridges crossing the Tiber are <a href="/wiki/Pons_Cestius" title="Pons Cestius">Ponte Cestio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Sant%27Angelo" title="Ponte Sant'Angelo">Ponte Sant'Angelo</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Milvio" title="Ponte Milvio">Ponte Milvio</a>. Considering <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Nomentano" title="Ponte Nomentano">Ponte Nomentano</a>, also built during ancient Rome, which crosses the <a href="/wiki/Aniene" title="Aniene">Aniene</a>, currently there are five ancient Roman bridges still remaining in the city.<sup id="cite_ref-204" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-204"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>200<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Other noteworthy bridges are <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Sisto" title="Ponte Sisto">Ponte Sisto</a>, the first bridge built in the Renaissance above Roman foundations; <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Rotto" class="mw-redirect" title="Ponte Rotto">Ponte Rotto</a>, actually the only remaining arch of the ancient <i>Pons Aemilius</i>, collapsed during the flood of 1598 and demolished at the end of the 19th century; and <a href="/wiki/Ponte_Vittorio_Emanuele_II" title="Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II">Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II</a>, a modern bridge connecting Corso Vittorio Emanuele and Borgo. Most of the city's public bridges were built in Classical or Renaissance style, but also in Baroque, Neoclassical and Modern styles. According to the <i><a href="/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica" title="Encyclopædia Britannica">Encyclopædia Britannica</a></i>, the finest ancient bridge remaining in Rome is the Ponte Sant'Angelo, which was completed in 135 AD, and was decorated with ten statues of the angels, designed by <a href="/wiki/Gian_Lorenzo_Bernini" title="Gian Lorenzo Bernini">Bernini</a> in 1688.<sup id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-205"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>201<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Catacombs">Catacombs</h4></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Catacombs_of_Rome" title="Catacombs of Rome">Catacombs of Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:PiusXItomb2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/PiusXItomb2.jpg/250px-PiusXItomb2.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/PiusXItomb2.jpg/500px-PiusXItomb2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3872" data-file-height="2592"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Vatican_Necropolis" title="Vatican Necropolis">Vatican Caves</a> are the location of many papal burials.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome has an extensive amount of ancient catacombs, or underground burial places under or near the city, of which there are at least forty, some discovered only in recent decades. Though most famous for Christian burials, they include <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_ancient_Rome" title="Religion in ancient Rome">pagan</a> and Jewish burials, either in separate catacombs or mixed together. The first large-scale catacombs were excavated from the 2nd century onwards. Originally they were carved through <a href="/wiki/Tuff" title="Tuff">tuff</a>, a soft <a href="/wiki/Volcanic_rock" title="Volcanic rock">volcanic rock</a>, outside the boundaries of the city, because <a href="/wiki/Roman_law" title="Roman law">Roman law</a> forbade burial places within city limits. Currently, maintenance of the catacombs is in the hands of the <a href="/wiki/Pope" title="Pope">Papacy</a> which has invested in the <a href="/wiki/Salesians_of_Don_Bosco" title="Salesians of Don Bosco">Salesians of Don Bosco</a> the supervision of the Catacombs of St. Callixtus on the outskirts of Rome.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Entertainment_and_performing_arts">Entertainment and performing arts</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Music_in_Rome" title="Music in Rome">Music in Rome</a> and <a href="/wiki/Events_in_Rome" class="mw-redirect" title="Events in Rome">Events in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Teatro_dell%27Opera_a_Roma.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Teatro_dell%27Opera_a_Roma.JPG/250px-Teatro_dell%27Opera_a_Roma.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Teatro_dell%27Opera_a_Roma.JPG/500px-Teatro_dell%27Opera_a_Roma.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3072" data-file-height="2304"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Teatro_dell%27Opera_di_Roma" title="Teatro dell'Opera di Roma">Teatro dell'Opera di Roma</a> at the Piazza Beniamino Gigli</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is an important centre for music, and it has an intense musical scene, including several prestigious music conservatories and theatres. It hosts the <a href="/wiki/Accademia_Nazionale_di_Santa_Cecilia" title="Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia">Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia</a> (founded in 1585), for which new concert halls have been built in the new <a href="/wiki/Parco_della_Musica" title="Parco della Musica">Parco della Musica</a>, one of the largest musical venues in the world. Rome also has an opera house, the <a href="/wiki/Teatro_dell%27Opera_di_Roma" title="Teatro dell'Opera di Roma">Teatro dell'Opera di Roma</a>, as well as several minor musical institutions. The city also played host to the <a href="/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_1991" title="Eurovision Song Contest 1991">Eurovision Song Contest</a> in 1991 and the <a href="/wiki/MTV_Europe_Music_Awards_2004" class="mw-redirect" title="MTV Europe Music Awards 2004">MTV Europe Music Awards</a> in 2004.
</p><p>Rome has also had a major impact on music history. The <a href="/wiki/Roman_School" title="Roman School">Roman School</a> was a group of composers of predominantly church music, which were active in the city during the 16th and 17th centuries, therefore spanning the late <a href="/wiki/Renaissance_music" title="Renaissance music">Renaissance</a> and early <a href="/wiki/Baroque_music" title="Baroque music">Baroque</a> eras. The term also refers to the music they produced. Many of the composers had a direct connection to the <a href="/wiki/Holy_See" title="Holy See">Vatican</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Sistine_Chapel" title="Sistine Chapel">papal chapel</a>, though they worked at several churches; stylistically they are often contrasted with the <a href="/wiki/Venetian_School_(music)" title="Venetian School (music)">Venetian School</a> of composers, a concurrent movement which was much more progressive. By far the most famous composer of the Roman School is <a href="/wiki/Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina" title="Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina">Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina</a>, whose name has been associated for four hundred years with smooth, clear, <a href="/wiki/Polyphony" title="Polyphony">polyphonic</a> perfection. However, there were other composers working in Rome, and in a variety of styles and forms.
</p><p>Between 1960 and 1970 Rome was considered to be as a "new Hollywood" because of the many actors and directors who worked there; Via Vittorio Veneto had transformed into a glamour place where you could meet famous people.<sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>202<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Fashion">Fashion</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fontana.della.barcaccia.arp.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Fontana.della.barcaccia.arp.jpg/250px-Fontana.della.barcaccia.arp.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="198" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Fontana.della.barcaccia.arp.jpg/500px-Fontana.della.barcaccia.arp.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2130" data-file-height="1687"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Via_Condotti" title="Via Condotti">Via Condotti</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is also widely recognised as a world <a href="/wiki/Fashion_capital" title="Fashion capital">fashion capital</a>. Although not as important as Milan, Rome is the fourth most important centre for fashion in the world, according to the 2009 <a href="/wiki/Global_Language_Monitor" title="Global Language Monitor">Global Language Monitor</a> after <a href="/wiki/Milan" title="Milan">Milan</a>, <a href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Paris" title="Paris">Paris</a>, and beating <a href="/wiki/London" title="London">London</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>203<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Major luxury fashion houses and jewellery chains, such as <a href="/wiki/Valentino_SpA" class="mw-redirect" title="Valentino SpA">Valentino</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bulgari" title="Bulgari">Bulgari</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fendi" title="Fendi">Fendi</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-208"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>204<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Laura_Biagiotti" title="Laura Biagiotti">Laura Biagiotti</a>, <a href="/wiki/Brioni_(brand)" title="Brioni (brand)">Brioni</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Renato_Balestra" title="Renato Balestra">Renato Balestra</a>, are headquartered or were founded in the city. Also, other major labels, such as <a href="/wiki/Gucci" title="Gucci">Gucci</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chanel" title="Chanel">Chanel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Prada" title="Prada">Prada</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dolce_%26_Gabbana" title="Dolce & Gabbana">Dolce & Gabbana</a>, <a href="/wiki/Armani" title="Armani">Armani</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Versace" title="Versace">Versace</a> have luxury boutiques in Rome, primarily along its prestigious and upscale <a href="/wiki/Via_Condotti" title="Via Condotti">Via dei Condotti</a>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Cuisine">Cuisine</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Roman_cuisine" title="Roman cuisine">Roman cuisine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Espaguetis_carbonara.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Espaguetis_carbonara.jpg/250px-Espaguetis_carbonara.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Espaguetis_carbonara.jpg/500px-Espaguetis_carbonara.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1365"></a><figcaption><i>Spaghetti <a href="/wiki/Carbonara" title="Carbonara">alla carbonara</a></i>, a typical Roman dish</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cacio_e_pepe.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Cacio_e_pepe.jpg/250px-Cacio_e_pepe.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="141" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Cacio_e_pepe.jpg/500px-Cacio_e_pepe.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3794" data-file-height="2136"></a><figcaption><span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it">Spaghetti <a href="/wiki/Cacio_e_pepe" title="Cacio e pepe">cacio e pepe</a></i></span>, a typical Roman dish</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome's cuisine has evolved through centuries and periods of social, cultural, and political changes. Rome became a major gastronomical centre during the <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">ancient age</a>. <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Roman_cuisine" title="Ancient Roman cuisine">Ancient Roman cuisine</a> was highly influenced by Ancient Greek culture, and after, the empire's enormous expansion exposed Romans to many new, provincial culinary habits and cooking techniques.<sup id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-209"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>205<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Later, during the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>, Rome became well known as a centre of high-cuisine, since some of the best chefs of the time worked for the popes. An example of this was <a href="/wiki/Bartolomeo_Scappi" title="Bartolomeo Scappi">Bartolomeo Scappi</a>, who was a chef working for <a href="/wiki/Pope_Pius_IV" title="Pope Pius IV">Pius IV</a>; he acquired fame in 1570 when his cookbook <i>Opera dell'arte del cucinare</i> was published. In the book he lists approximately 1,000 recipes of the Renaissance <a href="/wiki/Cuisine" title="Cuisine">cuisine</a> and describes cooking techniques and tools, giving the first known picture of a <a href="/wiki/Fork" title="Fork">fork</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-210"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>206<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Testaccio" title="Testaccio">Testaccio</a>, Rome's trade and slaughterhouse area, was often known as the "belly" or "slaughterhouse" of Rome, and was inhabited by butchers, or <i>vaccinari</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313-211"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>207<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The most common or ancient Roman cuisine included the "fifth quarter".<sup id="cite_ref-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313_211-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313-211"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>207<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The old-fashioned <i><a href="/wiki/Coda_alla_vaccinara" title="Coda alla vaccinara">coda alla vaccinara</a></i> (oxtail cooked in the way of butchers)<sup id="cite_ref-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313_211-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313-211"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>207<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is still one of the city's most popular meals and is part of most of Rome's restaurants' menus. Lamb is also a very popular part of Roman cuisine, and is often roasted with spices and herbs.<sup id="cite_ref-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313_211-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Eyewitness_Travel_2006_pg._312_-_313-211"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>207<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In the modern age, the city developed its own peculiar cuisine, based on products of the nearby <a href="/wiki/Roman_Campagna" title="Roman Campagna">Campagna</a>, <a href="/wiki/Artichoke" title="Artichoke">globe artichokes</a> are common.<sup id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-212"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>208<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In parallel, Roman Jews – present in the city since the 1st century BC – developed their own cuisine, the <i>cucina giudaico-romanesca</i>. The Roman cuisine widely use offal, resulting in dishes such as the entrail-based <a href="/wiki/Rigatoni" title="Rigatoni">rigatoni</a> with <span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it"><a href="/wiki/Rigatoni_con_la_Pajata" class="mw-redirect" title="Rigatoni con la Pajata">pajata</a></i></span> sauce. <span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it"><a href="/wiki/Abbacchio" title="Abbacchio">Abbacchio</a></i></span> is a meat dish based on lamb from the Roman cuisine.
</p><p>Examples of Roman dishes include <i><a href="/wiki/Saltimbocca" title="Saltimbocca">saltimbocca</a> alla romana</i> – a veal cutlet, Roman-style, topped with raw ham and sage and simmered with white wine and butter; <i><a href="/wiki/Carciofi_alla_romana" title="Carciofi alla romana">carciofi alla romana</a></i> – artichokes Roman-style, outer leaves removed, stuffed with mint, garlic, breadcrumbs and braised; <i><a href="/wiki/Carciofi_alla_giudia" title="Carciofi alla giudia">carciofi alla giudia</a></i> – artichokes fried in olive oil, typical of Roman Jewish cooking, outer leaves removed, stuffed with mint, garlic, breadcrumbs and braised; <i><a href="/wiki/Carbonara" title="Carbonara">spaghetti alla carbonara</a></i> – <a href="/wiki/Spaghetti" title="Spaghetti">spaghetti</a> with <a href="/wiki/Bacon" title="Bacon">bacon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Egg_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Egg (food)">eggs</a> and <span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it"><a href="/wiki/Pecorino_romano" title="Pecorino romano">pecorino romano</a></i></span>; <i><a href="/wiki/Cacio_e_pepe" title="Cacio e pepe">spaghetti cacio e pepe</a></i> – <a href="/wiki/Spaghetti" title="Spaghetti">spaghetti</a> with <span title="Italian-language text"><i lang="it"><a href="/wiki/Pecorino_romano" title="Pecorino romano">pecorino romano</a></i></span> and <a href="/wiki/Black_pepper" title="Black pepper">black pepper</a>; and <i><a href="/wiki/Gnocchi_alla_romana" title="Gnocchi alla romana">gnocchi di semolino alla romana</a></i> – <a href="/wiki/Semolina" title="Semolina">semolina</a> dumpling, Roman-style.<sup id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-213"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>209<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Cinema">Cinema</h3></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/List_of_films_set_in_Rome" title="List of films set in Rome">List of films set in Rome</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_films_set_in_ancient_Rome" title="List of films set in ancient Rome">List of films set in ancient Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ingressostorico_cinecitta.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Ingressostorico_cinecitta.jpg/250px-Ingressostorico_cinecitta.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Ingressostorico_cinecitta.jpg/500px-Ingressostorico_cinecitta.jpg 2x" data-file-width="850" data-file-height="567"></a><figcaption>Entrance to the <a href="/wiki/Cinecitt%C3%A0" title="Cinecittà">Cinecittà studios</a>, the largest film studio in <a href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">Europe</a><sup id="cite_ref-cinecittà_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cinecittà-214"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>210<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome hosts the <a href="/wiki/Cinecitt%C3%A0" title="Cinecittà">Cinecittà Studios</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-romefile1_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-romefile1-215"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>211<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> the largest film and television production facility in continental Europe and the centre of the <a href="/wiki/Cinema_of_Italy" title="Cinema of Italy">Italian cinema</a>, where many of today's biggest box office hits are filmed. The 99-acre (40 ha) studio complex is 9.0 km (5.6 mi) from the centre of Rome and is part of one of the biggest production communities in the world, second only to <a href="/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles,_California" class="mw-redirect" title="Hollywood, Los Angeles, California">Hollywood</a>, with well over 5,000 professionals – from period costume makers to visual effects specialists. More than 3,000 productions have been made on its lot.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2020)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup>
</p><p>Founded in 1937 by <a href="/wiki/Benito_Mussolini" title="Benito Mussolini">Benito Mussolini</a>, the studios were bombed by the <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Western Allies</a> during the Second World War. In the 1950s, Cinecittà was the filming location for several large American film productions, and subsequently became the studio most closely associated with <a href="/wiki/Federico_Fellini" title="Federico Fellini">Federico Fellini</a>. Today, Cinecittà is the only studio in the world with pre-production, production, and full post-production facilities on one lot, allowing directors and producers to walk in with their script and "walkout" with a completed film.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2020)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Sports">Sports</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:L%27Olimpico_-_panoramio.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/L%27Olimpico_-_panoramio.jpg/250px-L%27Olimpico_-_panoramio.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/L%27Olimpico_-_panoramio.jpg/500px-L%27Olimpico_-_panoramio.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1944"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Stadio_Olimpico" title="Stadio Olimpico">Stadio Olimpico</a>, home of <a href="/wiki/AS_Roma" title="AS Roma">AS Roma</a> and <a href="/wiki/SS_Lazio" title="SS Lazio">SS Lazio</a>, is one of the largest sports stadiums in Europe, with a capacity of over 70,000.<sup id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-216"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>212<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Association_football" title="Association football">Association football</a> is the most popular sport in Rome, as in the rest of the country. The city hosted the final games of the <a href="/wiki/1934_FIFA_World_Cup" title="1934 FIFA World Cup">1934</a> and <a href="/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup" title="1990 FIFA World Cup">1990 FIFA World Cup</a>. The latter took place in the <a href="/wiki/Stadio_Olimpico" title="Stadio Olimpico">Stadio Olimpico</a>, which is also the shared home stadium for local <a href="/wiki/Serie_A" title="Serie A">Serie A</a> clubs <a href="/wiki/SS_Lazio" title="SS Lazio">SS Lazio</a>, founded in 1900, and <a href="/wiki/AS_Roma" title="AS Roma">AS Roma</a>, founded in 1927, whose rivalry in the <a href="/wiki/Derby_della_Capitale" title="Derby della Capitale">Derby della Capitale</a> has become a staple of Roman sports culture.<sup id="cite_ref-217" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-217"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>213<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Footballers who play for these teams and are also born in the city tend to become especially popular, as has been the case with players such as <a href="/wiki/Francesco_Totti" title="Francesco Totti">Francesco Totti</a> and <a href="/wiki/Daniele_De_Rossi" title="Daniele De Rossi">Daniele De Rossi</a> (both for AS Roma), and <a href="/wiki/Alessandro_Nesta" title="Alessandro Nesta">Alessandro Nesta</a> (for SS Lazio).
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Stadio_dei_Marmi_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Stadio_dei_Marmi_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Stadio_dei_Marmi_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="125" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Stadio_dei_Marmi_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Stadio_dei_Marmi_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2000"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Stadio_dei_Marmi" title="Stadio dei Marmi">Stadio dei Marmi</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome hosted the <a href="/wiki/1960_Summer_Olympics" title="1960 Summer Olympics">1960 Summer Olympics</a>, with great success, using many ancient sites such as the <a href="/wiki/Villa_Borghese_gardens" title="Villa Borghese gardens">Villa Borghese</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Baths_of_Caracalla" title="Baths of Caracalla">Thermae of Caracalla</a> as venues. For the Olympic Games many new facilities were built, notably the new large Olympic Stadium (which was then enlarged and renewed to host several matches and the final of the <a href="/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup" title="1990 FIFA World Cup">1990 FIFA World Cup</a>), the <a href="/wiki/Stadio_Flaminio" title="Stadio Flaminio">Stadio Flaminio</a>, the Villaggio Olimpico (Olympic Village, created to host the athletes and redeveloped after the games as a residential district), ecc. Rome made a <a href="/wiki/Rome_bid_for_the_2020_Summer_Olympics" title="Rome bid for the 2020 Summer Olympics">bid</a> to host the <a href="/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics" title="2020 Summer Olympics">2020 Summer Olympics</a> but it was withdrawn.<sup id="cite_ref-olympic.org_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-olympic.org-218"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>214<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Bladesplace.id.au_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bladesplace.id.au-219"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>215<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Further, Rome hosted the <a href="/wiki/EuroBasket_1991" title="EuroBasket 1991">EuroBasket 1991</a> and is home to the internationally recognised basketball team <a href="/wiki/Virtus_Roma" title="Virtus Roma">Virtus Roma</a>. <a href="/wiki/Rugby_union" title="Rugby union">Rugby union</a> is gaining wider acceptance. Until 2011 the Stadio Flaminio was the home stadium for the <a href="/wiki/Italy_national_rugby_union_team" title="Italy national rugby union team">Italy national rugby union team</a>, which has been playing in the <a href="/wiki/Six_Nations_Championship" title="Six Nations Championship">Six Nations Championship</a> since 2000. The team now plays home games at the Stadio Olimpico because the Stadio Flaminio needs works of renovation in order to improve both its capacity and safety. Rome is home to local rugby union teams such as <a href="/wiki/Rugby_Roma_Olimpic" title="Rugby Roma Olimpic">Rugby Roma</a> (winner of five Italian championships), <a href="/wiki/Unione_Rugby_Capitolina" title="Unione Rugby Capitolina">Unione Rugby Capitolina</a> and <a href="/wiki/S.S._Lazio_Rugby_1927" title="S.S. Lazio Rugby 1927">S.S. Lazio Rugby 1927</a> (rugby union branch of the multisport club S.S. Lazio).
</p><p>Every May, Rome hosts the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Open_(tennis)" title="Italian Open (tennis)">Italian Open</a>, an <a href="/wiki/ATP_Masters_1000_tournaments" title="ATP Masters 1000 tournaments">ATP Masters 1000</a> tennis tournament, on the clay courts of the <a href="/wiki/Foro_Italico" title="Foro Italico">Foro Italico</a>. Cycling was popular in the post-World War II period, although its popularity has faded. Rome has hosted the final portion of the <a href="/wiki/Giro_d%27Italia" title="Giro d'Italia">Giro d'Italia</a> three times, in 1911, 1950, and 2009. Other local sports teams include volleyball (<a href="/wiki/M._Roma_Volley" title="M. Roma Volley">M. Roma Volley</a>), <a href="/wiki/Handball" title="Handball">handball</a> or <a href="/wiki/Water_polo" title="Water polo">waterpolo</a>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Transport">Transport</h2></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Transport_in_Rome" title="Transport in Rome">Transport in Rome</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Aeroporto_di_Roma-Fiumicino_in_2021.03.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Aeroporto_di_Roma-Fiumicino_in_2021.03.jpg/250px-Aeroporto_di_Roma-Fiumicino_in_2021.03.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Aeroporto_di_Roma-Fiumicino_in_2021.03.jpg/500px-Aeroporto_di_Roma-Fiumicino_in_2021.03.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3000"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci%E2%80%93Fiumicino_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Leonardo da Vinci–Fiumicino Airport">Leonardo da Vinci–Fiumicino Airport</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Giorcescivitavecchia3.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Giorcescivitavecchia3.JPG/250px-Giorcescivitavecchia3.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Giorcescivitavecchia3.JPG/500px-Giorcescivitavecchia3.JPG 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="600"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Port_of_Civitavecchia" title="Port of Civitavecchia">Port of Civitavecchia</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Rome is at the centre of the radial network of roads that roughly follow the lines of the ancient Roman roads which began at the <a href="/wiki/Capitoline_Hill" title="Capitoline Hill">Capitoline Hill</a> and connected Rome with its empire. Today central Rome is circled, at a distance of about 10 km (6 mi) from the Capitol, by the ring-road (the <a href="/wiki/Grande_Raccordo_Anulare" class="mw-redirect" title="Grande Raccordo Anulare">Grande Raccordo Anulare</a> or GRA).
</p><p>Due to its location in the centre of the Italian peninsula, Rome is the principal <a href="/wiki/Railway_node" title="Railway node">railway node</a> for central Italy. Rome's main railway station, <a href="/wiki/Roma_Termini_railway_station" title="Roma Termini railway station">Termini</a>, is one of the largest railway stations in Europe and the most heavily used in Italy, with around 400 thousand travellers passing through every day. The second-largest station in the city, <a href="/wiki/Roma_Tiburtina_railway_station" title="Roma Tiburtina railway station">Roma Tiburtina</a>, has been redeveloped as a <a href="/wiki/High-speed_rail_in_Italy" title="High-speed rail in Italy">high-speed rail</a> terminus.<sup id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-220"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>216<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As well as frequent high-speed day trains to all major Italian cities, Rome is linked nightly by 'boat train' sleeper services to Sicily, and internationally by overnight sleeper services to Munich and Vienna.
</p><p>Rome is served by three airports. The intercontinental <a href="/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci%E2%80%93Fiumicino_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Leonardo da Vinci–Fiumicino Airport">Leonardo da Vinci International Airport</a>, Italy's chief airport is located in the nearby <a href="/wiki/Fiumicino" title="Fiumicino">Fiumicino</a>, south-west of Rome. The older <a href="/wiki/Ciampino%E2%80%93G._B._Pastine_International_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Ciampino–G. B. Pastine International Airport">Rome Ciampino Airport</a> is a joint civilian and military airport. It is commonly referred to as "Ciampino Airport", as it is located beside <a href="/wiki/Ciampino" title="Ciampino">Ciampino</a>, south-east of Rome. A third airport, the <a href="/wiki/Rome_Urbe_Airport" title="Rome Urbe Airport">Rome Urbe Airport</a>, is a small, low-traffic airport located about 6 km (4 mi) north of the city centre, which handles most helicopter and private flights. The main city airport of Fiumicino, with over 49 million passengers transported in 2024, is the largest and busiest airport in Italy.
</p><p>Although the city has its own quarter on the Mediterranean Sea (<a href="/wiki/Ostia_(Rome)" title="Ostia (Rome)">Lido di Ostia</a>), this has only a marina and a small channel-harbour for fishing boats. The main harbour which serves Rome is <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Civitavecchia" title="Port of Civitavecchia">Port of Civitavecchia</a>, located about 62 km (39 mi) northwest of the city.<sup id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-221"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>217<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The city suffers from traffic problems largely due to this radial street pattern, making it difficult for Romans to move easily from the vicinity of one of the radial roads to another without going into the historic centre or using the ring-road. These problems are not helped by the limited size of Rome's metro system when compared to other cities of similar size. Rome has only 21 taxis for every 10,000 inhabitants, far below other major European cities.<sup id="cite_ref-222" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-222"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>218<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template noprint noexcerpt Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="data is out of date (January 2024)">better source needed</span></a></i>]</sup> Chronic congestion caused by cars during the 1970s and 1980s led to restrictions being placed on vehicle access to the inner city-centre during daylight hours. Areas, where these restrictions apply, are known as Limited Traffic Zones (<i>Zona a Traffico Limitato</i> (ZTL)). More recently, heavy night-time traffic in <a href="/wiki/Trastevere" title="Trastevere">Trastevere</a>, <a href="/wiki/Testaccio" title="Testaccio">Testaccio</a> and <a href="/wiki/San_Lorenzo_(Rome)" title="San Lorenzo (Rome)">San Lorenzo</a> has led to the creation of night-time ZTLs in those districts.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Roma_-_mappa_metropolitana_2025_(schematica).svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Roma_-_mappa_metropolitana_2025_%28schematica%29.svg/250px-Roma_-_mappa_metropolitana_2025_%28schematica%29.svg.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="127" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Roma_-_mappa_metropolitana_2025_%28schematica%29.svg/500px-Roma_-_mappa_metropolitana_2025_%28schematica%29.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1212" data-file-height="616"></a><figcaption>Rome Metro map updated to 2025 with the new Metro C stops of Porta Metronia and Colosseo</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Inaugurazione_metro_B1.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Inaugurazione_metro_B1.jpg/250px-Inaugurazione_metro_B1.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Inaugurazione_metro_B1.jpg/500px-Inaugurazione_metro_B1.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1728"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Conca_d%27Oro_(Rome_Metro)" title="Conca d'Oro (Rome Metro)">Conca d'Oro</a> metro station</figcaption></figure>
<p>A three-line metro system called the <i><a href="/wiki/Rome_Metro" title="Rome Metro">Metropolitana</a></i> operates in Rome. Construction on the first branch started in the 1930s.<sup id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-223"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>219<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The line had been planned to quickly connect the <a href="/wiki/Roma_Termini_railway_station" title="Roma Termini railway station">main railway station</a> with the newly planned E42 area in the southern suburbs, where 1942 the <a href="/wiki/List_of_world_expositions" class="mw-redirect" title="List of world expositions">World Fair</a> was supposed to be held. The event never took place because of war, but the area was later partly redesigned and renamed <a href="/wiki/EUR,_Rome" title="EUR, Rome">Esposizione Universale Roma</a> in the 1950s to serve as a modern business district. The line was finally opened in 1955, and it is now the south part of the B Line.
</p><p>The A line opened in 1980 from Ottaviano to Anagnina stations, later extended in stages (1999–2000) to Battistini. In the 1990s, an extension of the B line was opened from Termini to Rebibbia. The A and B lines intersect at Roma Termini station. A new branch of the B line (B1) opened on 13 June 2012 after an estimated building cost of €500 million. B1 connects to line B at Piazza Bologna and has four stations over a distance of 3.9 km (2 mi).
</p><p>A third line, the C line, is under construction with an estimated cost of €3 billion and will have 30 stations over a distance of 25.5 km (16 mi). It will partly replace the existing <a href="/wiki/Roma_Termini_railway_station" title="Roma Termini railway station">Termini</a>-Pantano rail line. It will feature full automated, driverless trains.<sup id="cite_ref-224" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-224"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>220<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The first section with 15 stations connecting Pantano with the quarter of Centocelle in the eastern part of the city, opened on 9 November 2014.<sup id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-225"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>221<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The end of the work was scheduled in 2015, but archaeological findings often delay underground construction work.
</p><p>A fourth line, D line, is also planned. It will have 22 stations over a distance of 20 km (12 mi). The first section was projected to open in 2015 and the final sections before 2035, but due to the city's financial crisis, the project has been put on hold.
</p><p>Above-ground public transport in Rome is made up of a bus, tram and urban train network (FR lines). The bus network has in excess of 350 bus lines and over eight thousand bus stops, whereas the more-limited tram system has 39 km (24 mi) of track and 192 stops.<sup id="cite_ref-226" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-226"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>222<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> There are also <a href="/wiki/Trolleybus" title="Trolleybus">trolleybuses</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-juts2009_227-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-juts2009-227"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>223<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
